title: The Black Cultural World System (working title)

entities.name: Robert Sengstacke Abbott
entities.description: Founder of the Chicago Defender (1905); Georgia-born migrant whose newspaper became the Great Migration's chief recruiting organ.

claims.claim: Robert S. Abbott was born on St. Simons Island, Georgia, moved to Chicago, trained in law, and began publishing the Chicago Defender in May 1905.
claims.evidence: BlackPast biography documents Abbott's Georgia birth, Chicago law training, and the Defender's May 1905 founding; Britannica corroborates the founding.
claims.source: Robert Sengstacke Abbott (1870-1940) George Tamblyn BlackPast

claims.claim: During World War I the Defender printed migration appeals, train schedules, and job listings, and railroad porters carried copies of the paper throughout the South, making it a direct instrument of the Great Migration.
claims.evidence: BlackPast notes the Defender's wartime migration coverage and porter-based distribution; Smithsonian Magazine's Pullman porter history corroborates porters' role as information carriers.
claims.source: Robert Sengstacke Abbott (1870-1940) George Tamblyn BlackPast
claims.uncertainty: Exact circulation and copy counts in the South vary across sources; the porter-distribution mechanism itself is consistently documented.

claims.claim: Abbott founded the Chicago Defender in 1905 and used it to orchestrate the Great Migration campaign.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record: 'Mr. Abbott preached in his editorials that the destiny of blacks was in the north, where factories were desperate for workers.'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Abbott and the Chicago branch of the NAACP led the opposition to Marcus Garvey within Chicago's African American community.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia of Chicago entry 'Garveyism': 'The Chicago branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and Robert S. Abbott, owner of the Chicago Defender, headed Garvey's opposition within Chicago's African American community.'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Ida B. Wells-Barnett
entities.description: Memphis anti-lynching journalist forced out of the South in 1892; resettled in Chicago and continued Southern investigative travel.

claims.claim: After a Memphis mob destroyed her Free Speech newspaper office in 1892, Ida B. Wells fled the South and settled in Chicago, where she worked with the Chicago Conservator and married Ferdinand Barnett.
claims.evidence: Wells's autobiography (quoted in Workers World) describes the 1892 destruction and her Chicago resettlement; historic-site materials corroborate.
claims.source: Crusade for Justice: The Autobiography of Ida B. Wells Ida B. Wells (ed. Alfreda Duster) Workers World (excerpt)

claims.claim: From her Chicago base, Wells continued traveling through the South to investigate lynchings firsthand, making her a circular-travel figure between Chicago and Southern sites of racial terror.
claims.evidence: Autobiography passages describe return trips South for lynching investigations; secondary historic-site summaries corroborate the pattern.
claims.source: Crusade for Justice: The Autobiography of Ida B. Wells Ida B. Wells University of Chicago Press (orig. 1970)
claims.uncertainty: Specific itineraries of individual Southern trips are not exhaustively catalogued in sources consulted.

claims.claim: Wells moved to Chicago in 1893 and lived there for the remainder of her life; she toured Britain in 1893 and 1894 as an anti-lynching speaker.
claims.evidence: British Newspaper Archive documents the 1893 and 1894 tours, invited by Catherine Impey and Isabella Fyvie Mayo; USC biography confirms the 1893 Chicago move.
claims.uncertainty: Low for the tours; the 1893 tour preceded or coincided with her Chicago relocation, so the 1894 tour is the clearer Chicago-linked transatlantic case.

claims.claim: Wells founded the Alpha Suffrage Club in Chicago in 1913 and marched in the 1913 Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington, D.C., refusing to march in a segregated section.
claims.evidence: USC biography (Alpha Suffrage Club, 1913); On This Day biography (1913 D.C. march).
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Wells briefly supported Garvey and the UNIA.
claims.evidence: Midwest Garveyism working paper, citing Paula Giddings (2008).
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: secondhand citation.

entities.name: Muddy Waters
entities.description: Mississippi Delta bluesman (McKinley Morganfield) who moved from Stovall Plantation to Chicago in 1943 and became the defining Chess Records artist. Chicago blues singer and guitarist (McKinley Morganfield, 1913–1983), central figure of the postwar Chicago electric blues sound.

claims.claim: Raised on Stovall Plantation near Clarksdale, Mississippi, Muddy Waters moved to Chicago in 1943 and began recording for the local label that became Chess Records.
claims.evidence: Britannica's biography records the Stovall upbringing, the 1943 Chicago move, and the Chess association.

claims.claim: Waters's amplified Delta blues defined the 'Chicago blues' style and made Chess Records the leading outlet for urban blues migrants from Mississippi.
claims.evidence: Britannica Money's Chess Records history names Waters among the Mississippi Delta artists who built the label's roster and the Chicago blues sound.
claims.source: Chess Records: From Muddy to 'Maybellene' Charlie Gillett Britannica Money

claims.claim: Muddy Waters toured the UK in 1958 with Chris Barber's band and pianist Otis Spann.
claims.evidence: uDiscover Music reports the 1958 UK tour with Barber and Spann.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary music-press source; needs corroboration from contemporary UK press or Barber's records before being treated as settled.

claims.claim: Muddy Waters performed at the first American Folk Blues Festival in 1962, including the Paris Olympia (20 October 1962) and Manchester Free Trade Hall (21 October 1962).
claims.evidence: Louder's history of the 1962 festival and Bear Family's festival documentation name Waters in the 1962 touring party; Ole Miss eGrove holds primary festival ephemera.
claims.source: Louder, 'First American Folk Blues Festival 1962 story' (loudersound.com); Bear Family (bear-family.com)
claims.uncertainty: Exact setlists for Waters at each 1962 date not captured.

entities.name: Howlin' Wolf
entities.description: Mississippi-born bluesman (Chester Burnett) who built his career in West Memphis before Leonard Chess brought him to Chicago in the winter of 1952-53. Chicago blues singer and guitarist (Chester Burnett, 1910–1976) who recorded in London in 1970 with British rock musicians.

claims.claim: Howlin' Wolf developed his radio and recording career in West Memphis; Memphis's Sam Phillips leased his recordings to Leonard Chess in Chicago, and Wolf relocated to Chicago in the winter of 1952-53.
claims.evidence: AllMusic biography documents the West Memphis period, the Phillips-Chess leasing arrangement, and the Chicago move; liner-note materials corroborate.

claims.claim: Chess had to compete with other companies that Phillips had also supplied with Wolf recordings, showing Memphis and Chicago labels bidding for the same Delta migrant artist.
claims.evidence: Biographical accounts describe the multi-label competition for Wolf after the Phillips-supplied recordings circulated.
claims.uncertainty: Details of the competing offers are thinly sourced; the Phillips-to-Chess pipeline itself is well documented.

claims.claim: In May 1970 Howlin' Wolf recorded The London Howlin' Wolf Sessions at Olympic Sound Studios, London, with Eric Clapton, Steve Winwood, Bill Wyman, and Charlie Watts; the album was remixed in Chicago.
claims.evidence: Discogs release metadata documents the London recording with the named British musicians and the Chicago remix.
claims.source: Discogs, 'The London Howlin' Wolf Sessions' release page (discogs.com)
claims.uncertainty: Discogs is user-submitted discographic data; session dates need corroboration from studio logs or contemporary press.

claims.claim: Howlin' Wolf was among the Chicago blues artists brought to Europe by the American Folk Blues Festival network in the 1960s.
claims.evidence: The University of Mississippi eGrove exhibit on the festival identifies Howlin' Wolf among the Chicago-linked participants.
claims.uncertainty: Which exact festival editions featured him was not captured.

entities.name: Thomas A. Dorsey
entities.description: Georgia-born 'father of gospel music' whose repeated Atlanta-Chicago moves ended in a permanent 1919 Chicago settlement; Pilgrim Baptist music director and gospel-convention founder.

claims.claim: Dorsey migrated back and forth between Atlanta and Chicago several times before settling in Chicago in 1919, a documented case of circular migration preceding permanent settlement.
claims.evidence: An FSU-repository thesis on Dorsey (citing Harris and Levine) documents the repeated Atlanta-Chicago moves and the 1919 settlement.
claims.source: Thomas A. Dorsey thesis Florida State University repository FSU DigiNole

claims.claim: Thomas A. Dorsey became music director of Chicago's Pilgrim Baptist Church (sources give 1931 or 1932) and developed gospel music there.
claims.evidence: The FSU thesis and Los Angeles Sentinel coverage document both 1932 milestones; historical-marker materials corroborate.
claims.source: Thomas A. Dorsey thesis Florida State University repository FSU DigiNole
claims.uncertainty: Appointment year varies by source (1931 vs 1932); the appointment itself is well documented.

claims.claim: As 'Georgia Tom,' Dorsey partnered with Tampa Red (Hudson Whittaker, born Smithville, Georgia, also Chicago-settled) on the 1928 hit 'It's Tight Like That,' linking Georgia blues migrants in Chicago's recording industry.
claims.evidence: Blues discographies and biographical sources document the Georgia Tom-Tampa Red partnership and the 1928 recording.
claims.source: Tampa Red / Georgia Tom discography Various blues discographical sources
claims.uncertainty: Partnership and recording are well attested; sales figures for 'It's Tight Like That' vary across sources.

entities.name: Sun Ra
entities.description: Birmingham, Alabama-born bandleader who arrived in Chicago in early 1946, formed the Arkestra on the South Side, and returned to Birmingham at life's end. Jazz big band led by Sun Ra (Herman Blount), developed in Chicago in the 1950s; first toured Europe in 1970–1971.

claims.claim: Sun Ra (Herman Blount) was born in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1914 and arrived in Chicago in early 1946, where his South Side work included stints with Wynonie Harris and Fletcher Henderson before he formed the Arkestra and founded Saturn Records.
claims.evidence: William Sites's 'Sun Ra's Chicago' research and a Spectrum Culture review document the Birmingham birth, the early-1946 Chicago arrival, and the South Side career arc.
claims.source: Sun Ra's Chicago William Sites urban-studies research

claims.claim: After suffering a stroke in 1990, Sun Ra returned to Birmingham to be cared for by family and died there in 1993 - a documented late-life return migration from Chicago to the South.
claims.evidence: Biographical sources document the 1990 stroke, the Birmingham return, and the 1993 death.
claims.source: Sun Ra biography Various biographical sources

claims.claim: Sun Ra's first concerts outside the United States took place in late summer and autumn 1970, with performances in France, Germany, and the UK.
claims.evidence: Strut Records (K7 Music, Berlin/London) liner notes for the 'Egypt 1971' release state the first non-US concerts occurred in late summer/autumn 1970 in France, Germany, and the UK; the HHV record-store listing repeats the same documented history.
claims.uncertainty: No venue-level detail captured in this research; the claim rests on label-produced liner notes.

claims.claim: A second European tour was arranged for late 1971; at its end Ra flew from Denmark to Cairo, where December 1971 recordings became the 'Live in Egypt' LPs.
claims.evidence: Same Strut Records liner notes document the late-1971 second European tour and the cheap flights from Denmark to Cairo, with recordings made in Giza, Heliopolis, and Cairo in December 1971.

entities.name: Elijah Muhammad
entities.description: Georgia-born leader who moved the Nation of Islam's headquarters from Detroit to Chicago after 1934, the strongest Detroit-to-Chicago institutional transfer found. Leader of the Nation of Islam (1934-1975), headquartered in Chicago; traveled through Africa and the Middle East in 1959-1960.

claims.claim: Elijah Poole (later Elijah Muhammad) was born in Georgia, moved with his family to Detroit in 1923, joined the Nation of Islam after Wallace Fard's appearance in 1930, and relocated the movement's leadership to Chicago - establishing Temple No. 2 and a new headquarters - amid Detroit factionalism following Fard's 1934 disappearance.
claims.evidence: EBSCO Research Starters and the African American Registry document the Georgia birth, the 1923 Detroit move, and the post-1934 Chicago relocation.
claims.source: Elijah Muhammad EBSCO EBSCO Research Starters

claims.claim: From November 1959 to January 1960, Elijah Muhammad undertook a world tour that included Turkey, Pakistan, Syria, Sudan, Egypt, Ethiopia, Lebanon, Jordan and Saudi Arabia, where he performed Umrah.
claims.evidence: Peer-reviewed article in Religions (MDPI, 2019) documents the itinerary and the Umrah.
claims.source: Black Religion and Black Power: The Nation of Islam's Internationalism
claims.uncertainty: Low for the itinerary; the article is the single peer-reviewed source located so far. Red-team: rests on a single secondary source; needs independent corroboration.

claims.claim: During the 1959-60 tour Elijah Muhammad met Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser, according to the Nation of Islam's own newspaper account.
claims.evidence: The NOI's newspaper (Final Call) account of the tour reports the Nasser meeting; the tour itinerary itself is confirmed by the MDPI article.
claims.source: Black Religion and Black Power: The Nation of Islam's Internationalism (context); NOI newspaper tour account
claims.uncertainty: The meeting claim comes from the NOI's own organ and lacks independent corroboration.
claims.contradictory_evidence: No independent (non-NOI) source for the meeting has been located.

claims.claim: Elijah Muhammad moved the Nation of Islam's center from Detroit to Chicago after 1934, establishing Temple No. 2 as headquarters.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia.com; AJIS peer-reviewed article (1985).
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Jesse L. Jackson Sr.
entities.description: Greenville, South Carolina-born minister who came to Chicago for seminary study and built Operation Breadbasket and Operation PUSH there. Chicago-based civil rights leader; visited South Africa in 1979 to denounce apartheid and hosted ANC president Oliver Tambo at PUSH headquarters.

claims.claim: Born in Greenville, South Carolina, Jesse Jackson studied at Chicago Theological Seminary; in 1966 Martin Luther King Jr. appointed him to head SCLC's Operation Breadbasket in Chicago.
claims.evidence: A CNN timeline and Greenville Business Magazine profile document the Greenville birth, the Chicago seminary study, and the 1966 Breadbasket appointment.

claims.claim: In December 1971 Jackson founded Operation PUSH in Chicago, creating a durable Chicago-based national civil-rights organization.
claims.evidence: The CNN timeline and Greenville Business Magazine date PUSH's Chicago founding to December 1971.

claims.claim: In 1979 Rev. Jesse Jackson visited South Africa, where he publicly denounced apartheid as 'ungodly' and a 'terroristic dictatorship.'
claims.evidence: Multiple biographical/news sources (thepoint.gm; sankofaonline) report the 1979 South Africa visit and anti-apartheid statements; illinoisdelivered (2026 obituary) quotes Washington Post coverage of the visit.
claims.source: Who is Rev Jesse Jackson Sr.? (thepoint.gm); Rev. Jesse Jackson obituary (illinoisdelivered)
claims.uncertainty: Low-moderate; multiple consistent secondary sources, no primary itinerary located.

claims.claim: ANC president Oliver Tambo appeared with Jackson at Operation PUSH headquarters in Chicago.
claims.evidence: illinoisdelivered obituary includes a photo caption: 'The Rev. Jesse Jackson and Oliver Tambo, president of the African National Congress... respond to cheers at Operation PUSH headquarters.'
claims.source: Rev. Jesse Jackson, civil rights leader and Chicago icon, dead at 84
claims.uncertainty: Single captioned photograph; date of the PUSH HQ meeting not given.

entities.name: Langston Hughes
entities.description: Harlem-based writer whose weekly Chicago Defender column carried his Harlem workingman character Jesse B. Semple to a national Black readership for decades. Harlem Renaissance writer who co-translated Nicolás Guillén into English in 1948 while writing a weekly column for the Chicago Defender (1942–62), giving the translation a Chicago Black-press conduit.

claims.claim: Langston Hughes wrote a weekly column for the Chicago Defender, 1942–1962, featuring Jesse B. Semple.
claims.evidence: University of Missouri Press edition metadata and a scholarly OpenEdition chapter document the Defender column and the February 1943 Simple debut.
claims.source: The Collected Works of Langston Hughes / Simple scholarship University of Missouri Press MUP
claims.uncertainty: Track A gave a February 1943 start; 1942 is the historically standard date. Reconciled at merge; confirm against Hughes scholarship/Defender archives.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Kirkus review dates the first Simple column to 1942.

claims.claim: Hughes and Ben F. Carruthers published the first English translations of Nicolás Guillén's poetry as Cuba Libre (Anderson & Ritchie, 1948), during Hughes's Defender-column years.
claims.evidence: The Academy of American Poets (poets.org) Guillén profile records the 1948 Cuba Libre translation by Hughes and Carruthers.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: single source located; no evidence was found that the translation's publication itself was a Chicago venture, so the Chicago nexus rests on the Defender column overlap, not on the book's imprint.

entities.name: Richard Wright
entities.description: Mississippi-born writer who fled Memphis for Chicago on December 27, 1927, and wrote Native Son out of the Chicago Black Belt experience. Chicago writer (1908–1960), author of Native Son (1940); moved permanently to France in 1947 and lived in Paris until his death.

claims.claim: Richard Wright was born near Natchez, Mississippi, in 1908, grew up in Memphis, and left Memphis for Chicago on December 27, 1927, at age nineteen, working as a postal worker and street sweeper.
claims.evidence: EBSCO Research Starters documents the December 27, 1927 Memphis-to-Chicago move; GradeSaver and FCPS biographical materials corroborate the Mississippi birth and Chicago jobs.
claims.source: Black Boy and American Hunger EBSCO EBSCO Research Starters

claims.claim: Wright published Native Son in 1940 after moving to New York in 1937; he wrote the introduction to Drake and Cayton's Black Metropolis (1945), linking Chicago's literary and sociological documentation of the migration.
claims.evidence: EBSCO and GradeSaver document the 1940 publication and 1937 New York move; the KU journal article on Drake documents Wright's Black Metropolis introduction.
claims.source: Black Boy and American Hunger; The Roots and Routes of 'Imperium in Imperio' EBSCO; Andrew J. Rosa EBSCO; Kansas University journals

claims.claim: Wright moved to Chicago's South Side in 1927, worked in the Federal Writers' Project, and published Uncle Tom's Children (1938) and Native Son (1940); he first visited Paris in May 1946 as a guest of the French government and settled in France permanently with his family in 1947.
claims.evidence: Harvard philosopher Tommie Shelby's chapter (citing the University of Chicago Press biography) documents the 1947 permanent move; a Wright chronology records the May 1946 French-government visit and the 1947 permanent expatriation.
claims.source: Tommie Shelby, 'Richard Wright: Realizing the Promise of the West' (tommieshelby.com, citing U. of Chicago Press); 'A Richard Wright Chronology' (maps-legacy.org)
claims.uncertainty: Shelby's chapter is a scholarly secondary source; the chronology is an enthusiast site — the corroboration is one-directional and should be strengthened with the cited biography.

claims.claim: In Paris, Wright wrote the screenplay for the film version of Native Son and starred in it as Bigger Thomas; he later published The Outsider (1953) and reported on the Bandung Conference (The Color Curtain, 1955).
claims.evidence: Book notes on Wright and the Wright chronology document the Native Son film script and starring role, The Outsider (1953), and the Bandung reporting.
claims.source: 'Book Notes: Richard Wright's Native Son & Black Boy' (docs.preterhuman.net); 'A Richard Wright Chronology' (maps-legacy.org)
claims.uncertainty: Both are tertiary/enthusiast sources; the Native Son film role is, however, widely documented.

claims.claim: Wright died in Paris on 28 November 1960 and was buried in Père-Lachaise cemetery.
claims.evidence: The Wright chronology records the 28 November 1960 death and the Père-Lachaise burial (cremation 3 December).
claims.uncertainty: One source gave the date as 28 February 1960, which appears to be an error; the November date is corroborated by the book-notes source.
claims.contradictory_evidence: A SweetSearch biography page states Wright died 'of a heart attack on Feb. 28, 1960' — contradicted by the chronology and book notes (November 28, 1960).

entities.name: Willie Dixon
entities.description: Vicksburg, Mississippi-born songwriter, producer, and bassist who moved to Chicago in 1936 and became Chess Records' studio architect. Chicago blues songwriter, producer, and bassist (1915–1992) whose compositions became UK chart hits via British rock covers.

claims.claim: Willie Dixon was born in Vicksburg, Mississippi, on July 1, 1915, and moved to Chicago in 1936, where he first pursued boxing before turning to music full time.
claims.evidence: The Mississippi Blues Trail marker (msbluestrail.org) documents the Vicksburg birth and the 1936 Chicago move.
claims.source: Willie Dixon - Vicksburg Mississippi Blues Trail msbluestrail.org

claims.claim: Dixon joined Chess Records' staff in 1951 as house bassist, arranger, songwriter, and producer, writing standards for Muddy Waters ('Hoochie Coochie Man'), Howlin' Wolf ('Little Red Rooster,' 'Back Door Man'), Little Walter, and others.
claims.evidence: The Mississippi Blues Trail and Britannica Money's Chess history document Dixon's 1951 Chess staff role and his songwriting for the label's stars.
claims.source: Willie Dixon - Vicksburg; Chess Records: From Muddy to 'Maybellene' Mississippi Blues Trail; Charlie Gillett msbluestrail.org; Britannica Money

claims.claim: Dixon wrote 'Little Red Rooster', first recorded by Howlin' Wolf as 'The Red Rooster' for Chess in 1961; the Rolling Stones' cover was released as a UK single on 13 November 1964 and spent one week at No. 1 on the UK Singles Chart in December 1964.
claims.evidence: Facility Fun's song history documents the Dixon authorship, the Howlin' Wolf 1961 Chess recording, the 13 November 1964 UK single release, and the December week at No. 1; Men's Journal (citing uDiscover Music) records the No. 1 week beginning 3 December 1964 and five weeks in the UK Top 10.
claims.source: Facility Fun, 'When The Rolling Stones Ruled The Roost' (facilityfun.com), 2024-09-02; Men's Journal (mensjournal.com), 2026-09-02
claims.uncertainty: Sources disagree on the exact No. 1 week (3 December vs 5 December 1964); the chart-topping fact itself is consistent across sources.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Some fan sources claim the track was recorded at Chess Studios, Chicago; the two music histories place the recording at Regent Sound, London, on 2 September 1964, and note the recording exists only in mono.

claims.claim: 'Little Red Rooster' was the first blues record to top the British pop charts.
claims.evidence: Facility Fun states it remains the only blues song to have topped the British pop charts; a YouTube discographic description independently states it was the first blues record to top the charts in Britain.
claims.uncertainty: The 'only/first ever' framing depends on genre definitions; treated as a claim about chart history, not a settled encyclopedic fact.

claims.claim: Dixon recorded with Fleetwood Mac and other Chicago blues musicians at Chess's Ter-Mar studio in Chicago on 4 January 1969.
claims.evidence: Discogs release metadata for the Fleetwood Mac/Chicago blues session documents the 4 January 1969 Ter-Mar recording and Dixon's participation.
claims.uncertainty: Discogs is user-submitted; session date needs corroboration.

claims.claim: The first American Folk Blues Festival tour came together through Willie Dixon's connections.
claims.evidence: Louder's festival history states the 1962 tour came together via Dixon.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; Dixon's precise organizational role not detailed.

entities.name: Marcus Garvey
entities.description: Jamaican-born, Harlem-based UNIA leader who brought his movement to Chicago in September 1919, electrifying the South Side Black Belt.

claims.claim: In September 1919 Marcus Garvey traveled from UNIA headquarters in Harlem to Chicago to sell Black Star Line stock; he addressed 250 people at the Eighth Illinois Regiment armory on the South Side on September 28, 1919, and was arrested and fined for violating Chicago's Blue Sky Laws.
claims.evidence: Biographical accounts (ujamaalive.africa) document the September 1919 Chicago trip and the Blue Sky Law arrest; UIUC professor Erik McDuffie's study documents the September 28, 1919 armory address.
claims.contradictory_evidence: A working paper asserts an earlier first visit by 1917; the 1919 trip itself is well documented.

claims.claim: Thousands of Black Chicagoans joined the UNIA in the early 1920s; the Chicago movement, with Black women playing a critical organizing role, later spawned Black nationalist political and religious movements in the city.
claims.evidence: McDuffie's peer-reviewed study 'Chicago, Garveyism, and the history of the diasporic Midwest' documents the mass Chicago membership and its afterlives.
claims.source: Chicago, Garveyism, and the history of the diasporic Midwest Erik S. McDuffie University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (African American Studies/History)

claims.claim: Jamaican-born Marcus Garvey founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) in 1914; by 1920 the UNIA had several Chicago divisions, principally on the South Side, holding weekly Liberty Hall meetings and operating businesses.
claims.evidence: The Encyclopedia of Chicago states Garvey founded the UNIA in Jamaica in 1914 and that by 1920 the organization had several Chicago divisions with weekly Liberty Hall meetings; the scholarly paper 'Garveyism and the Midwest' corroborates the Chicago organizing.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago (encyclopedia.chicagohistory.org/pages/502.html); 'Garveyism and the Midwest' (crossculturalsolidarity.com PDF)
claims.uncertainty: Moderate on the number of divisions and membership figures, which vary across accounts; the PDF places Division 23 at 4859 S. State, founded 1920. Do not infer members' island origins without evidence.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Membership estimates for Chicago divisions vary and should be treated with caution.

claims.claim: Claimed first Chicago visit by 1917 (working paper) — DISPUTED: the best-documented foundational visit is September 1919.
claims.evidence: Midwest Garveyism working paper.
claims.uncertainty: Low.
claims.contradictory_evidence: UIUC scholarship documents a September 1919 Black Star Line stock trip as the foundational visit; no pre-1919 visit independently verified.

claims.claim: Division 23 president William A. Wallace served as a delegate to the UNIA's First International Convention of Negro Peoples of the World in Harlem in 1920 and became UNIA secretary-general in 1926.
claims.evidence: Midwest Garveyism working paper.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Chicago Defender
entities.description: Black weekly newspaper founded in Chicago in 1905; the Great Migration's most important print recruiting and information network. Historic Chicago Black newspaper; published solidarity coverage of Ethiopia (1930s) and Sharpeville/apartheid (1960).

claims.claim: The Chicago Defender was first published in May 1905 by Robert S. Abbott and during World War I actively encouraged Southern Black migration with job listings, train schedules, and success stories, distributed across the South by Pullman porters.
claims.evidence: BlackPast's Abbott biography documents the May 1905 founding and the wartime migration campaign with porter distribution.
claims.source: Robert Sengstacke Abbott (1870-1940) George Tamblyn BlackPast

claims.claim: Langston Hughes's weekly 'Simple' column ran in the Defender from February 1943 for decades, making the Chicago paper a national literary platform for a Harlem writer.
claims.evidence: University of Missouri Press and OpenEdition scholarship document the column's 1943 start and long run.
claims.source: Simple scholarship University of Missouri Press MUP
claims.uncertainty: Canonical Hughes record reconciles the column run to 1942–1962 (1942 is the historically standard start date); confirm against Defender archives.

claims.claim: On March 24, 1960, the Chicago Daily Defender published the editorial/report 'Massacre in South Africa,' describing Sharpeville as 'wanton slaughtering' and 'white supremacy in bloody display.'
claims.evidence: Georgetown University thesis quoting the Defender's March 24, 1960 'Massacre in South Africa' editorial.
claims.source: Georgetown thesis on the Chicago Defender and apartheid
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The Defender published an open letter framing Ethiopia as 'the oldest Christian nation' resisting Italian aggression, building Black American solidarity with Ethiopia during the Italo-Ethiopian war.
claims.evidence: Global Histories journal article analyzing the Defender's Ethiopia coverage, including the open letter and Joel Augustus Rogers's pro-Ethiopia writing.
claims.source: Global Histories article on African American press and Ethiopia
claims.uncertainty: Low-moderate; student journal, but quoting primary press text.

claims.claim: The Chicago Defender was founded in Chicago on May 5, 1905 by Robert Sengstacke Abbott.
claims.evidence: Illinois House Resolution 93-HR0406 and Congressional Record tributes record the May 5, 1905 founding by Robert Sengstacke Abbott.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The Defender's 'Great Northern Drive' campaign drew Southern readers north and helped drive the Great Migration, with over 1 million African Americans reading vivid descriptions of life in the North in its pages.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record centennial tribute: 'The Defender led a remarkable campaign which brought thousands of southerners to the north from 1915 to 1925. Known in the history books as the Great Migration, over 1 million African Americans read vivid descriptions about options to life in the south in the pages of the Defender.'
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: the claim is a political tribute's characterization; scholarly sources (e.g., Cambridge Church History article on Abbott's 'Great Northern Drive') corroborate the migration-advocacy role. Red-team: sourced to Congressional Record centennial tributes (honorific genre), not scholarship.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; scale estimates vary across scholarship.

claims.claim: By 1929 the Defender was selling more than 250,000 copies each week.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record centennial tribute: 'By 1929, the Defender was selling more than 250,000 copies each week.'
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: single government-source figure; treat as peak estimate, not independently audited. Red-team: sourced to Congressional Record centennial tributes (honorific genre), not scholarship.

entities.name: Chess Records
entities.description: Chicago record label (Aristocrat 1947, renamed Chess 1950) built by Leonard and Phil Chess on Mississippi Delta migrants; home of Chicago blues and early rock and roll. Chicago record label (2120 South Michigan Avenue) whose studios hosted visiting British rock bands in the 1960s.

claims.claim: In 1947 Leonard Chess became a partner in Chicago's Aristocrat Record Company; by 1950 he and his brother Phil had bought out the other partners and renamed it Chess Records, shifting its focus to down-home blues by artists such as Muddy Waters.
claims.evidence: Britannica Money's Chess history (updated July 31, 2026) documents the 1947 Aristocrat partnership, the 1950 renaming, and the blues pivot.
claims.source: Chess Records: From Muddy to 'Maybellene' Charlie Gillett Britannica Money

claims.claim: Chess's roster drew overwhelmingly on migrants from the Mississippi Delta - Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Sonny Boy Williamson II, Little Walter, Bo Diddley - plus St. Louis's Chuck Berry; bassist-arranger Willie Dixon was the studio's vital behind-the-scenes presence.
claims.evidence: Britannica Money names the Delta-born roster and Dixon's role; the Mississippi Blues Trail corroborates Dixon's Chess position.
claims.source: Chess Records: From Muddy to 'Maybellene' Charlie Gillett Britannica Money

claims.claim: Chess obtained Southern talent through Memphis's Sam Phillips, who supplied recordings by Howlin' Wolf, Rufus Thomas, and others - a documented Memphis-to-Chicago recording pipeline.
claims.evidence: Biographical and label histories document the Phillips-to-Chess supply arrangement.
claims.source: Leonard Chess / Chess Records histories Various label histories

claims.claim: The Rolling Stones recorded at Chess Studios, Chicago, on 10–11 June 1964; the band later named an instrumental '2120 South Michigan Avenue' after the studio's address.
claims.evidence: Elsewhere's account of the 1964 session quotes Bill Wyman's and Charlie Watts's recollections of recording at Chess.
claims.uncertainty: Session details rest on musician recollections quoted in a music-press feature.

claims.claim: On 4 January 1969 Fleetwood Mac and Chicago blues musicians (Otis Spann, Willie Dixon, Shakey Horton, J.T. Brown, Buddy Guy, Honeyboy Edwards, S.P. Leary) recorded at Chess's Ter-Mar studio; the session was released by the UK label Blue Horizon in December 1969 as Blues Jam at Chess.
claims.evidence: Discogs release metadata documents the personnel, the Ter-Mar studio, the January 1969 date, and the December 1969 Blue Horizon release.
claims.uncertainty: Discogs is user-submitted; release month and session date need corroboration from Blue Horizon discography.

entities.name: Nation of Islam
entities.description: Religious and political movement founded in Detroit (1930) whose headquarters moved to Chicago after 1934 under Elijah Muhammad. Chicago-headquartered Black religious and political movement with documented travel, financial and broadcast links to Africa and the Middle East.

claims.claim: Following Wallace Fard's 1934 disappearance and Detroit factionalism, Elijah Muhammad relocated the Nation of Islam's leadership to Chicago, establishing Temple No. 2 and a new national headquarters there.
claims.evidence: EBSCO Research Starters and the African American Registry document the post-1934 Detroit-to-Chicago relocation.
claims.source: Elijah Muhammad EBSCO EBSCO Research Starters

claims.claim: The Nation of Islam was headquartered in Chicago under Elijah Muhammad (1934-1975) and maintained direct African links: Elijah Muhammad's 1959-60 tour of Africa and the Middle East, Malcolm X's 1959 emissary travel, and the 1985 Gaddafi loan and satellite address.
claims.evidence: MDPI Religions (2019) for the 1959-60 tour and Malcolm X's 1959 travel; secondary accounts and Congressional Record (1996) for the Libya relationship.
claims.source: Black Religion and Black Power: The Nation of Islam's Internationalism; Congressional Record
claims.uncertainty: The travel links are well documented; the financial specifics are provisional. Shared rhetoric alone is not treated as the link — only travel, funds, and the satellite address. Red-team: no primary financial document located; sources ideologically loaded. Kept as Unresolved, excluded from relationship graph.
claims.contradictory_evidence: The Gaddafi financial details rest on partisan/secondary sources.

claims.claim: After W. D. Fard's disappearance in 1934, Elijah Muhammad moved followers from Detroit to Chicago and made Temple No. 2 the movement's headquarters.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia.com biography of Elijah Muhammad; peer-reviewed 1985 article (AJIS).
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Operation PUSH
entities.description: Chicago-based civil-rights organization founded by Jesse Jackson in December 1971, growing out of SCLC's Operation Breadbasket. Chicago-based civil rights organization founded by Jesse Jackson; a platform for his anti-apartheid advocacy.

claims.claim: Jesse Jackson founded Operation PUSH (People United to Save Humanity) in Chicago in December 1971 after heading SCLC's Operation Breadbasket in the city from 1966.
claims.evidence: A CNN timeline and Greenville Business Magazine profile document the December 1971 founding and the Breadbasket predecessor.

claims.claim: Rev. Jesse Jackson founded Operation PUSH (People United to Save Humanity) in Chicago in 1971; it merged with the National Rainbow Coalition in 1996 to form the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition.
claims.evidence: sankofaonline and thepoint.gm biographies: founded Operation PUSH in Chicago in 1971; merged 1996 into Rainbow/PUSH.
claims.uncertainty: Low-moderate.

claims.claim: Jackson's platform included opposition to apartheid; he challenged apartheid in his 1988 Democratic convention concession speech and ANC president Oliver Tambo appeared with him at PUSH headquarters in Chicago.
claims.evidence: uatl.com: 1988 concession speech 'challenged apartheid in South Africa'; illinoisdelivered photo caption: Jackson and Tambo 'at Operation PUSH headquarters.'
claims.source: In Atlanta, Jesse Jackson found a home and a stage; Jackson obituary
claims.uncertainty: The Tambo-at-PUSH-HQ detail rests on a single photo caption without a date.

entities.name: Johnson Publishing Company
entities.description: Chicago-based Black publishing company founded by John H. Johnson; Ebony (1945) and Jet (1951) gave Chicago a national Black press voice. Chicago-based Black publishing company (Ebony, Jet); sent correspondents to Africa and covered African leaders.

claims.claim: John H. Johnson built Johnson Publishing Company in Chicago, launching Ebony in 1945 and Jet in 1951.
claims.evidence: Ebony's own retrospectives document the Chicago base and the 1945/1951 launches.

claims.claim: Jet's September 15, 1955 issue published David Jackson's photographs of Emmett Till's open casket - the first wide circulation of the image - by decision of publisher John H. Johnson with Mamie Till-Mobley's permission.
claims.evidence: The Emmett Till Project and Ebony document the September 15, 1955 publication, the photographer, and the Johnson/Mobley decisions.
claims.source: Giving Up the Ghost of National Myth and Dangerous Fictions Dr. Samuel K. Roberts Emmett Till Project

claims.claim: Johnson Publishing Company, based in Chicago, published Ebony magazine, for which Era Bell Thompson traveled through 18 African countries in 1953 as a foreign correspondent.
claims.evidence: African American Registry and Rutgers dissertation on Thompson's Ebony career and 1953-54 Africa travel narrative.
claims.source: Era Thompson helped shape Ebony magazine
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Jet magazine, published in Chicago by Johnson Publishing, put Kenyan leader Tom Mboya on its cover on April 30, 1959 ('Africa's New Leader') during his U.S. tour.
claims.evidence: Prior research documented Jet's April 30, 1959 Mboya cover story during his U.S. tour.
claims.uncertainty: Cover documented in prior research pass; issue not re-verified in this session. The coverage link is Chicago-Africa media, not a Chicago visit.
claims.contradictory_evidence: No evidence that Mboya visited Chicago on the 1959 tour (see negative findings).

claims.claim: Johnson Publishing Company was founded in Chicago in 1942; the first issue of Ebony appeared on November 1, 1945, and circulation grew to over two million.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tributes document the 1942 founding, the November 1, 1945 first issue, and circulation above two million.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Ebony and its sister magazine Jet published Emmett Till's open-casket photographs in September 1955, carrying the Chicago funeral into national and international view.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record: Jet 'published the open-casket images of Emmett Till, a decision to let the world see' the Till lynching's aftermath; Ebony covered the funeral at Roberts Temple.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Associated Negro Press
entities.description: Chicago-based Black wire service founded by Claude Barnett in 1919; supplied news to Black newspapers nationally and internationally. Chicago-based international Black press service; maintained African correspondents and covered African independence movements.

claims.claim: Claude Barnett - born in Sanford, Florida, Tuskegee Institute class of 1906, then a Chicago postal clerk - founded the Associated Negro Press in Chicago in 1919 as a wire service for African American newspapers.
claims.evidence: Stanford's King Institute (citing the King Papers) documents Barnett's Florida birth, Tuskegee graduation, Chicago move, and the 1919 ANP founding.
claims.source: To Claude Barnett Stanford King Institute kinginstitute.stanford.edu (King Papers)

claims.claim: The ANP grew into the first and largest national news service for Black newspapers, with correspondents and writers in all major centers of Black population, supplying twice-weekly packets domestically and eventually to African papers.
claims.evidence: Nieman Reports' Black press timeline and encyclopedia summaries document the ANP's national scale and correspondent network.
claims.source: Timeline: Milestones of the Black Press in the U.S. Nieman Reports niemanreports.org

claims.claim: The Associated Negro Press was a Chicago-based international Black news organization under Claude Barnett, prioritizing foreign reporting on Africa; its Chicago headquarters and African correspondent Bankole ('Bankhold') Timothy — photographed with Kwame Nkrumah — are identified in a Library of Congress newsreel inventory.
claims.evidence: Gerald Horne, The Rise and Fall of the Associated Negro Press (UI Press, 2017); LOC item mbrs01841243 (via YouTube description) identifies ANP's Chicago headquarters and correspondent Timothy with Nkrumah.
claims.source: The Rise and Fall of the Associated Negro Press; LOC newsreel inventory mbrs01841243
claims.uncertainty: Low for the ANP's Chicago base and African network; the Timothy surname spelling is uncertain.
claims.contradictory_evidence: The correspondent's surname spelling ('Bankole' vs 'Bankhold' Timothy) is uncertain.

claims.claim: Claude Barnett founded the Associated Negro Press in Chicago in 1919; its office was at 312 South Clark Street, Chicago.
claims.evidence: Stanford King Institute: Barnett founded ANP in Chicago in 1919. Wikipedia's ANP article (with cited references) gives the 312 South Clark Street office address.
claims.uncertainty: Low for founding; the street address is corroborated only by a secondary encyclopedia source.

claims.claim: The ANP employed African American foreign correspondents and maintained bureaus in Washington, New York, London, at the UN, and in Africa by 1953.
claims.evidence: Library of Congress inventory of the 1953 newsreel 'One Tenth of a Nation – The Press' identifies ANP's Chicago headquarters and correspondents: Samuel Perry at the United Nations, Alice Dunnigan as White House correspondent, Bankhold Timothy covering Africa (seen with Kwame Nkrumah), Samuel Morris covering Europe from London, and Gladys Graham covering New York.
claims.uncertainty: Low: contemporaneous documentary evidence.

claims.claim: The ANP served about 150 U.S. Negro newspapers and 100 newspapers in Africa in French and English.
claims.evidence: This exact figure appears in the Wikipedia ANP article (cited to a print source) and is repeated in derivative sources; Gerald Horne's 2017 University of Illinois Press book 'The Rise and Fall of the Associated Negro Press' characterizes the ANP as an international news organization with African correspondents, but the precise 150/100 counts have not been independently confirmed from the primary or peer-reviewed literature in this research round.
claims.uncertainty: High: exact subscriber counts are weakly sourced.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found, but no independent confirmation.

entities.name: Claude Barnett
entities.description: Chicago journalist and head of the Associated Negro Press; built a Chicago-based international news network serving Africa and advised African governments.

claims.claim: Claude Barnett headed the Chicago-based Associated Negro Press, which became an international Black news organization covering Africa; he helped send doctors and teachers to Africa and advised African governments.
claims.evidence: Gerald Horne's The Rise and Fall of the Associated Negro Press (University of Illinois Press, August 2017) documents Barnett's Chicago-based ANP as an international Black news organization and his Africa advisory work.
claims.source: The Rise and Fall of the Associated Negro Press: Claude Barnett's Pan-African News and the Jim Crow Paradox
claims.uncertainty: Low for the ANP's scope; specific correspondence details await archive-level verification.

claims.claim: Barnett traveled through multiple African countries in 1960 and helped Supreme Life Insurance of Chicago host visitors from 19 African countries in 1961.
claims.evidence: Biographical account on originalpeople.org describes the 1960 travel and the 1961 Supreme Life hosting.
claims.uncertainty: Weak source; needs corroboration from Horne's book or newspaper archives before Verified.

claims.claim: Barnett and his wife Etta Moten Barnett attended Ghanaian independence celebrations in 1957; Etta interviewed Martin Luther King Jr. there on March 6, 1957.
claims.evidence: Stanford King Institute profile of Claude Barnett records both Barnetts' attendance at the 1957 Ghanaian independence celebrations and Etta Moten Barnett's March 6, 1957 interview of Martin Luther King Jr.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Barnett attended the 1958 All-African People's Conference in Accra, Ghana.
claims.evidence: African Activist Archive lists Claude Barnett among Americans at the 1958 All-African People's Conference in Accra.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Barnett published responses from Liberian president William V. S. Tubman and Senator John F. Kennedy in an ANP release dated March 28, 1960.
claims.evidence: Stanford King Institute documents the ANP release of March 28, 1960 carrying responses from Tubman and Kennedy.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Muhammad Speaks
entities.description: Chicago-published Nation of Islam newspaper (1960-1975); a major Black-press platform for African liberation coverage.

claims.claim: Muhammad Speaks, the Nation of Islam's newspaper, was published from Chicago (1963 issue imprint: 'Chicago, Mohammad's Mosque No. 2') and became one of the most widely read Black newspapers of the 1960s-70s, with circulation reported at 500,000-600,000 weekly.
claims.evidence: 1963 issue imprint (Ridge Books listing); Sapelo Square analysis (2026): circulation surpassing 500,000 weekly, outpacing the Pittsburgh Courier; Trinity UCC history: over 600,000.
claims.source: Muhammad Speaks, July 19 1963 (listing); Beyond Borders (Sapelo Square)
claims.uncertainty: Low for Chicago publication and scale; founding-by-Malcolm-X detail remains provisional.

claims.claim: In the 1960s-70s Muhammad Speaks was a leading outlet for African decolonization coverage: it sent reporters to nations in Africa, Asia and Latin America to cover liberation movements, and nearly all major leaders of liberation movements and progressive governments in the global South subscribed, according to editor John Woodford.
claims.evidence: Doctoral thesis (HAL science, on Muhammad Speaks 1960-1975): reporters sent to many nations in Africa, Asia, Latin America to cover liberation/decolonization; Sapelo Square: global South liberation leaders subscribed per editor John Woodford; Free Library article: April 1967 coverage of Dennis Brutus's anti-apartheid Olympics campaign.
claims.source: African American Women Militantism in the Nation of Islam Through Muhammad Speaks; Beyond Borders; African Americans, Pan-Africanism, and the anti-apartheid campaign
claims.uncertainty: Low-moderate; thesis-level scholarship plus corroborating analyses. Open question: unverified whether coverage was original reporting or reprinted wire copy; needs byline/dateline sampling of digitized issues.

claims.claim: Muhammad Speaks began in Harlem in 1960 as 'Mr. Muhammad Speaks,' moved to Chicago in 1961, shortened its title, and became a nationally circulated weekly newspaper of the Nation of Islam.
claims.evidence: JSTOR Daily and a French doctoral thesis document the 1960 Harlem founding, the 1961 move to Chicago, and national circulation; BlackPast documents NOI member distribution networks and 400,000 weekly copies by late 1969.
claims.uncertainty: Low for the Harlem-to-Chicago transfer and national circulation; foundership is contested between Malcolm X- and Elijah Muhammad-centered narratives.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Founding narratives differ (Malcolm X vs. Elijah Muhammad); the move and circulation are not disputed.

entities.name: Chicago Sister Cities International
entities.description: City of Chicago's official sister-cities program; formal municipal link to Accra, Durban and Casablanca. City program coordinating Chicago's sister-city relationships, including the Mexico City (est. 1991) and Bogotá committees.

claims.claim: Chicago Sister Cities International, a division of World Business Chicago, maintains sister-city relationships with three African cities: Casablanca, Morocco (1982); Accra, Ghana (1989); and Durban, South Africa (1997).
claims.evidence: CSCI announcement (via thearabdailynews, 2014) listing all 28 sister cities with years: 'Accra, Ghana (1989)... Casablanca, Morocco (1982)... Durban, South Africa (1997).'
claims.source: Chicago Sister Cities International named Best Overall
claims.uncertainty: Low for the pairings and years.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None for the dates and pairings.

claims.claim: The Chicago-Casablanca committee documented concrete exchanges: a 1991 reaffirmation with a Casablanca delegation led by the Wali of Casablanca Ahmed Motii and six Moroccan governors; a 1992 culture program; a youth service project pairing seven Chicago teenagers with seven Moroccan youth in Casablanca (later reciprocated in Chicago); and a permanent mural at O'Hare's international terminal.
claims.evidence: CSCI's own 'Type of Exchange' history for Casablanca (chicagosistercities.com PDF).
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Mayor Richard M. Daley's Executive Order 1990-90-1 created the citywide Chicago Sister Cities program to coordinate exchanges of people, ideas, culture, education, and trade; City Council records mark the Chicago–Mexico City relationship's 25th anniversary in 2016, implying establishment in 1991; joint Bogotá/Mexico City committee programming included a screening of 'Gabo: The Creation of Gabriel García Márquez.'
claims.evidence: Executive Order 1990-90-1 (City of Chicago, primary document); CSCI Mexico City and Bogotá committee histories (2016).
claims.uncertainty: Low on the executive order and Mexico City dating (inferred from 25th anniversary); moderate on the precise formalization date of the Bogotá relationship.

entities.name: Chicago, Illinois
entities.description: Anchor city of the track: recording center (Chess/Checker, Universal Recording Corp.), Black press center (Chicago Defender), home of Puerto Rican Chicago, and node for Black Atlantic scholarship via the University of Chicago and Northwestern.

claims.claim: Chicago is the receiving city for the Caribbean migration, music, festival, and institutional exchanges documented in this track.
claims.evidence: All entities in this track are documented in relation to Chicago, Illinois: Caribbean communities in Rogers Park/Uptown/Woodlawn, Jamaican and Haitian consular offices, Caribbean-founded festivals, reggae venues, and Caribbean music performances and exhibitions in the city.
claims.uncertainty: None for the geographic anchor; bilateral link strength varies per entity.

claims.claim: Chicago served as a recording and institutional anchor for documented Black–Latin American musical and scholarly exchanges, including the March 2, 1955 recording of 'Bo Diddley' at Universal Recording Studio, 46 E. Walton Street, and the founding of the Center for Black Music Research at Columbia College Chicago.
claims.evidence: Session discographies place the Checker 814 session at Universal Recording Studio, 46 E. Walton Street, Chicago, on March 2, 1955; the CBMR was founded at Columbia College Chicago in 1983 with a mission covering Black music worldwide.
claims.uncertainty: Low on the facts cited; the cultural-interpretation claims (clave lineage, diasporic framing) are handled separately as Provisional.

entities.name: Katherine Dunham
entities.description: Chicago-trained dancer, choreographer, and anthropologist whose Brazilian-themed stage works and 1950 Brazil tour form two of the track's strongest documented Chicago ↔ Brazil links. Chicago-based dancer, choreographer, and anthropologist (1909–2006) whose company toured Europe from 1948.

claims.claim: Dunham, trained in anthropology at the University of Chicago, created the Brazilian/Bahian-themed works Bahiana (1939) and Batucada (1940), the latter appearing in Warner Bros.' Carnival of Rhythm (1941); scholarship holds she had not yet visited Brazil and drew on recordings, cultural images, and Caribbean embodied knowledge.
claims.evidence: Peer-reviewed Dance Research Journal article on Dunham's repertory and its African-diasporic imagination.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: single peer-reviewed source located in this session; the 'not yet visited Brazil' point and the exact source materials are the article's findings and should not be overstated.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; popular accounts sometimes imply direct Brazilian fieldwork, which this scholarship qualifies.

claims.claim: Dunham toured Brazil in 1950 at the invitation connected to the Black Experimental Theater (Teatro Experimental do Negro); her São Paulo hotel-discrimination case was reported in Correio Paulistano in July 1950 and became a catalyst for the Lei Afonso Arinos.
claims.evidence: NPR (2016) places Dunham in São Paulo in 1950 visiting the Black Experimental Theater; the American Society of History, Arts and Letters article cites Correio Paulistano's July 11 and 13, 1950 coverage of her public denunciation.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Dunham's professional career began in Chicago in 1938; her company made its first European tour in 1948, including London, followed by return engagements in France and Italy.
claims.evidence: A Harvard repository document on Dunham records the 1938 Chicago start, the 1948 first European tour with London, and the French and Italian returns.
claims.uncertainty: Document type not fully verified (appears to be a scholarly paper or thesis); needs archival corroboration.

claims.claim: Dunham is reported to have said that Europe 'saved her company' — a statement about her own company's finances, not a general claim about Black American art or the blues.
claims.evidence: The attribution was noted in session research but the primary source of the quotation was not captured.
claims.source: Attribution not captured in session sources
claims.uncertainty: The exact wording, context, and source of the quotation need primary sourcing; do not generalize it into a 'Europe saved Black culture' narrative.

entities.name: Louis Armstrong
entities.description: New Orleans cornetist summoned to Chicago in 1922 by King Oliver; the move anchored the New Orleans-Chicago jazz corridor.

claims.claim: In 1922 King Oliver, already leading the Creole Jazz Band in Chicago, sent for Louis Armstrong in New Orleans; Armstrong joined the band in Chicago, later moved to New York to play with Fletcher Henderson, and then returned to Chicago.
claims.evidence: A commonly cited telegram from Oliver to Armstrong ('If you're not doing anything come on up here. You can make plenty money') is reproduced in biographical sources; the 1922 Chicago arrival is standard in Armstrong chronologies.
claims.source: Louis Armstrong biography Various last.fm (artist biography)
claims.uncertainty: This pass did not locate an archival or university-press source for the 1922 summons; the telegram text is widely repeated but its provenance needs confirmation.

entities.name: Joe "King" Oliver
entities.description: New Orleans/Louisiana bandleader who relocated to Chicago in 1919 and built the Creole Jazz Band, the bridge for the New Orleans-Chicago jazz migration.

claims.claim: King Oliver moved from Louisiana to Chicago in 1919, formed the Creole Jazz Band, and in 1922 summoned Louis Armstrong from New Orleans to join him.
claims.evidence: Standard jazz histories date Oliver's Chicago arrival to 1919 and the Armstrong summons to 1922; corroboration beyond encyclopedia and fan sources is still needed.
claims.source: King Oliver biography Various sittingbull blog / oldtimeblues.net
claims.uncertainty: Authoritative archival sourcing for the 1919 arrival and 1922 summons was not located in this pass; treat as provisional pending Chicago History Museum or Smithsonian verification.

entities.name: Mahalia Jackson
entities.description: New Orleans-born gospel singer who moved to Chicago as a teenager and became the voice linking Chicago gospel to the national civil-rights movement.

claims.claim: Mahalia Jackson moved from New Orleans to Chicago at about age sixteen, joined the Greater Salem Baptist Church choir, and began a roughly fourteen-year touring and recording partnership with Thomas A. Dorsey.
claims.evidence: Louisiana Weekly biographical coverage and standard Jackson biographies document the move, the church choir, and the Dorsey partnership.
claims.source: Mahalia Jackson biography Louisiana Weekly Louisiana Weekly
claims.uncertainty: Arrival year is given as 1927 in most sources and 1928 in at least one; treat 1927 as favored but not certain.
claims.contradictory_evidence: At least one secondary biography dates the move to 1928 rather than 1927.

claims.claim: Jackson sang Thomas A. Dorsey's 'Take My Hand, Precious Lord' at Martin Luther King Jr.'s funeral in Atlanta in 1968, carrying a Chicago gospel composition into the movement's central mourning ritual.
claims.evidence: Louisiana Weekly coverage of Jackson's career documents the 1968 funeral performance.
claims.source: Mahalia Jackson biography Louisiana Weekly Louisiana Weekly

entities.name: Sam Cooke
entities.description: Clarksdale, Mississippi-born singer whose family moved to Chicago in 1933; developed through Chicago gospel quartets into soul music stardom.

claims.claim: Sam Cooke was born in Clarksdale, Mississippi, in 1931; his family moved to Chicago in 1933, where he sang with the Singing Children, the Highway QCs, and then the Soul Stirrers.
claims.evidence: Delta Blues Museum and BlackPast biographies document the 1931 Clarksdale birth, the 1933 Chicago move, and the quartet progression.
claims.source: Sam Cooke biography Delta Blues Museum Delta Blues Museum

entities.name: Nat King Cole
entities.description: Montgomery, Alabama-born pianist-singer whose family settled in Chicago's Bronzeville in 1923; absorbed the Defender's youth culture and South Side jazz.

claims.claim: Nat King Cole was born in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1919; his family moved to Chicago in 1923 and settled in Bronzeville, where he encountered the Chicago Defender's Bud Billiken programs and the South Side jazz scene.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia of Alabama and an EBSCO biography document the 1919 Montgomery birth, the 1923 Chicago move, and the Bronzeville upbringing.
claims.source: Nat King Cole biography Encyclopedia of Alabama Encyclopedia of Alabama

entities.name: Dinah Washington
entities.description: Tuscaloosa, Alabama-born singer raised in Chicago; church and club development led to a Regal Theater talent-contest discovery.

claims.claim: Dinah Washington was born in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, in 1924; her family moved to Chicago when she was about four. She developed through St. Luke's Baptist Church, Sallie Martin's gospel group, and Chicago clubs before winning a talent contest at the Regal Theater.
claims.evidence: A University of Alabama news feature and an EBSCO biography document the Tuscaloosa birth, the childhood Chicago move, and the church-to-Regal progression.
claims.source: Dinah Washington biography University of Alabama UA News

entities.name: Roebuck "Pops" Staples
entities.description: Winona, Mississippi-born patriarch of the Staple Singers; Mississippi-to-Chicago migrant whose family group later recorded for Memphis's Stax.

claims.claim: Pops Staples was born near Winona, Mississippi, and moved with his family to Chicago as part of the Great Migration, where he worked in meatpacking, steel, and construction while continuing gospel music and eventually forming the Staple Singers with his children.
claims.evidence: The NEA Masters of Traditional Arts profile documents the Winona birth, the Chicago move, the industrial jobs, and the family's gospel formation.
claims.source: Pops Staples: Masters of Traditional Arts National Endowment for the Arts NEA
claims.uncertainty: The migration year is reported as 1935 in some NEA materials and 1936 in others; musicologist Rob Bowman's biography implies 1941 ('four years after' 1937). The year is disputed.
claims.contradictory_evidence: NEA sources give 1935 or 1936; Rob Bowman's artist biography states Staples was with the Golden Trumpets of Drew, Mississippi in 1937 and moved to Chicago four years later (i.e., 1941).

claims.claim: The Chicago-based Staple Singers recorded early gospel for Chicago's Vee-Jay Records and in 1968 signed with Memphis-based Stax Records, recording with Steve Cropper and Booker T. & the MG's - a documented Chicago-to-Memphis recording flow.
claims.evidence: Rob Bowman's artist biography and Craft Recordings' Stax Collection liner materials document the Vee-Jay gospel sides and the 1968 Stax signing.
claims.source: The Staple Singers artist biography Rob Bowman Believers Portal

claims.claim: The family's first road work out of Chicago included dates in New Orleans and Jackson, Mississippi, a documented reverse cultural flow from Chicago back to the South.
claims.evidence: The NEA Masters of Traditional Arts profile notes the early Southern touring dates.
claims.source: Pops Staples: Masters of Traditional Arts National Endowment for the Arts NEA

entities.name: John Lee Hooker
entities.description: Mississippi-born bluesman who settled in Detroit in 1943 and recorded repeatedly in Chicago for the Black-owned Vee-Jay label.

claims.claim: John Lee Hooker, born in Mississippi, moved to Detroit in 1943 and later recorded in Chicago for Vee-Jay Records, including the album Burnin' cut in Chicago on October 26, 1961.
claims.evidence: Discographic sources document the 1943 Detroit move and the October 26, 1961 Chicago session for Vee-Jay.
claims.source: John Lee Hooker sessionography Various discographical sources
claims.uncertainty: Session date and personnel details rest on discographic compilations; seek Vee-Jay session logs or Bear Family liner notes for confirmation.

claims.claim: Hooker's Vee-Jay single 'Boom Boom' used Detroit's Funk Brothers - including James Jamerson and Benny Benjamin - on a Chicago recording, a documented Detroit-Chicago studio collaboration.
claims.evidence: Session personnel listings credit Jamerson and Benjamin on the Chicago 'Boom Boom' session.
claims.source: Boom Boom session personnel Various discographical sources
claims.uncertainty: Musician-level session credits for this era are reconstructed from aural and archival evidence; treat personnel as provisional.

entities.name: A. Philip Randolph
entities.description: Florida-born labor leader who organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters from New York; the union's Chicago division became a migration-era power base.

claims.claim: A. Philip Randolph, born in Florida and based in Harlem, founded and led the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters in 1925; Chicago organizers Milton P. Webster and John C. Mills built the union's powerful Chicago division through mass meetings.
claims.evidence: DC Historic Sites and DePaul Pressbooks labor histories document Randolph's New York leadership and the Webster/Mills Chicago organizing.
claims.source: Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters history Various DC Historic Sites; DePaul Pressbooks

claims.claim: Randolph later directed the 1963 March on Washington, extending the porters' Chicago-New York labor network into national civil-rights action.
claims.evidence: Standard civil-rights histories document Randolph's direction of the 1963 march.
claims.source: March on Washington history Various civil-rights histories

entities.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
entities.description: Atlanta-based SCLC leader whose organization joined Chicago's Black freedom struggle in the 1965-66 Chicago Freedom Movement.

claims.claim: King's Atlanta-headquartered SCLC partnered with Chicago's Coordinating Council of Community Organizations (CCCO) in the Chicago Freedom Movement of 1965-66; King rented an apartment in North Lawndale in January 1966, led Freedom Sunday at Soldier Field on July 10, 1966, and marched in Marquette Park in August 1966.
claims.evidence: A Chicago Housing Authority historical PDF and a Habitat for Humanity Portland summary document the SCLC-CCCO partnership, the North Lawndale apartment, Freedom Sunday, and the Marquette Park march.
claims.source: Chicago Freedom Movement history Chicago Housing Authority CHA historical PDF
claims.uncertainty: This pass did not consult Stanford's King Institute papers for the campaign; the two sources used agree on the core facts.

claims.claim: Mahalia Jackson, the Chicago gospel singer, sang at King's funeral in Atlanta in 1968, closing a Chicago-Atlanta loop opened by the 1966 campaign.
claims.evidence: Louisiana Weekly coverage documents Jackson's 1968 funeral performance.
claims.source: Mahalia Jackson biography Louisiana Weekly Louisiana Weekly

entities.name: Emmett Till
entities.description: Fourteen-year-old Chicagoan murdered while visiting relatives near Money, Mississippi, in August 1955; his Chicago funeral became a national catalyst.

claims.claim: Emmett Till, a Chicago youth, was visiting relatives near Money, Mississippi, in August 1955 when he was abducted and murdered after an encounter at Bryant's Grocery; his mother insisted his body be returned to Chicago.
claims.evidence: The U.S. Department of Justice case overview documents the Chicago residence, the Money, Mississippi visit, the August 1955 abduction and murder, and the return of the body.
claims.source: Emmett Till case overview U.S. Department of Justice justice.gov
claims.uncertainty: The precise nature of the alleged offense at Bryant's Grocery is disputed across historical accounts; the abduction and murder themselves are established.

claims.claim: This is a case of circular family travel - not migration - with lethal consequences, illustrating the continued vulnerability of Northern Black families in the South.
claims.evidence: Analytical framing grounded in the DOJ case facts and the Emmett Till Project's scholarship.
claims.source: Emmett Till Project Dr. Samuel K. Roberts emmetttillproject.com

entities.name: Mamie Till-Mobley
entities.description: Chicago mother whose open-casket funeral decision and cooperation with Jet magazine turned her son's murder into a movement catalyst.

claims.claim: Mamie Till-Mobley had her son's body returned to Chicago and insisted on an open-casket funeral at Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ, attended by a reported 50,000 people.
claims.evidence: Ebony's retrospective and the Emmett Till Project document the return of the body, the open-casket decision, and the funeral attendance figure.
claims.source: Remembering Emmett Till's Brutal Murder Ebony ebony.com

claims.claim: With her permission, Chicago-based Jet magazine published photographs of Till's body in its September 15, 1955 issue, taken by Jet staff photographer David Jackson at the A.A. Rayner Funeral Home.
claims.evidence: The Emmett Till Project (Dr. Samuel K. Roberts) and Ebony both document the September 15, 1955 Jet publication and the photographer's identity.
claims.source: Giving Up the Ghost of National Myth and Dangerous Fictions Dr. Samuel K. Roberts Emmett Till Project

entities.name: Margaret Walker
entities.description: Birmingham-born poet who built her career in 1930s Chicago and then returned South, joining Jackson State College's faculty in 1949 - a named Chicago-to-South return.

claims.claim: Margaret Walker was born in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1915, moved with family to New Orleans, then north to Chicago, where she earned a B.A. from Northwestern in 1935, worked for the Federal Writers' Project (1936-39), and joined Richard Wright's South Side Writers Group, eventually leading it after Wright moved to New York.
claims.evidence: Jackson State University's Margaret Walker Center biography documents the Birmingham birth, the Chicago education and WPA work, and the South Side Writers Group leadership.
claims.source: Margaret Walker biography (Appendix H) Jackson State University dev.jsums.edu (Margaret Walker Center)

claims.claim: In 1949 Walker moved to Jackson, Mississippi, to join the English faculty at Jackson State College, where she taught until 1979 and in 1968 founded one of the nation's first Black Studies institutes - a documented, named return migration from the Northern Black metropolis to the South.
claims.evidence: JSU Newsroom and the University of Alabama's Alabama Authors archive document the 1949 faculty appointment, the 30-year tenure, and the 1968 institute founding.
claims.source: Margaret Walker Center centennial JSU Newsroom jsumsnews.com

entities.name: Ida Mae Brandon Gladney
entities.description: Mississippi sharecropper who migrated to Chicago in 1937; her documented working-class family story anchors the non-celebrity migration experience.

claims.claim: Ida Mae Brandon Gladney left sharecropping in Chickasaw County, Mississippi, for Chicago in 1937 with her husband George; George hauled ice and Ida Mae did domestic work before becoming a hospital aide, and the couple eventually bought a home on Chicago's South Side.
claims.evidence: Isabel Wilkerson's The Warmth of Other Suns (2010) documents the 1937 migration, the jobs, and the South Side home purchase; an NPR/WKU interview with Wilkerson corroborates.
claims.source: The Warmth of Other Suns Isabel Wilkerson Random House

entities.name: Chuck Berry
entities.description: St. Louis guitarist who traveled to Chicago in May 1955, was referred by Muddy Waters to Leonard Chess, and recorded 'Maybellene' - the St. Louis-Chicago rock-and-roll corridor.

claims.claim: Chuck Berry, born in St. Louis in 1926, traveled to Chicago in May 1955 seeking a recording contract; after seeing Muddy Waters perform, Waters directed him to Leonard Chess, who signed him and recorded 'Maybellene' on May 21, 1955.
claims.evidence: The Alabama Record Collectors Association's session history and Britannica-derived biographies document the St. Louis origin, the May 1955 Chicago trip, Waters's referral, and the May 21 recording date.
claims.source: Birth of Rock & Roll Music Project: 1955: Chuck Berry: Maybellene Alabama Record Collectors Association alabamarecordcollectors.org

entities.name: Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters
entities.description: First Black-led labor union chartered by the AFL (1925); organized the Pullman porters whose Chicago division became a migration-era institution.

claims.claim: A. Philip Randolph founded the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters in 1925 from New York; Chicago organizers Milton P. Webster and John C. Mills built the Chicago division through mass meetings, giving the Pullman Company's Chicago-based workforce a union.
claims.evidence: DC Historic Sites and DePaul Pressbooks labor histories document the 1925 founding, Randolph's New York leadership, and the Webster/Mills Chicago organizing.
claims.source: Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters history Various DC Historic Sites; DePaul Pressbooks

claims.claim: The porters, employed by the Chicago-headquartered Pullman Company, formed a human information network between Chicago and the South, carrying newspapers (including the Defender), news, and culture in both directions.
claims.evidence: Smithsonian Magazine's Pullman porter history corroborates the porters' information-carrying role; BlackPast documents the Defender distribution specifically.
claims.source: Five Things to Know About Pullman Porters Smithsonian Magazine smithsonianmag.com

entities.name: Illinois Central Railroad
entities.description: Chicago-headquartered railroad whose north-south mainline (Chicago-New Orleans via Mississippi, with Memphis branches) was the Great Migration's principal physical corridor.

claims.claim: The Illinois Central's principal lines ran Chicago-Mattoon-Carbondale-Grenada, Mississippi-New Orleans, with branches Memphis-Vicksburg-Baton Rouge-New Orleans and Memphis-Greenwood-Jackson, Mississippi; its largest passenger terminal was Central Station in Chicago.
claims.evidence: American-Rails.com's Illinois Central history tabulates the routes and the Chicago Central Station headquarters.
claims.source: Illinois Central Railroad: Map, Logo, History American-Rails.com american-rails.com

claims.claim: The railroad's Gulf-to-Great-Lakes route made its passenger trains a means of transport during the Great Migration, funneling Mississippi, Tennessee, and Louisiana migrants into Chicago.
claims.evidence: Trains.com's Illinois Central history describes the north-south system; the migration-transport role is widely asserted in railroad histories.
claims.source: Illinois Central Railroad: A history Trains trains.com
claims.uncertainty: The route facts are verified; the specific claim about the scale of migrant ridership rests on general historical consensus rather than a located ridership study in this pass.

entities.name: Vee-Jay Records
entities.description: Black-owned Chicago record label founded in 1953 by Vivian Carter and Jimmy Bracken; recorded Detroit-based John Lee Hooker and the Chicago Staple Singers.

claims.claim: Vee-Jay Records was launched in 1953 by Vivian Carter and her husband Jimmy Bracken, a married Black couple who set up shop on Chicago's South Side; Smithsonian Magazine calls it the most successful Black-run record company before Motown in Detroit.
claims.evidence: Smithsonian Magazine (Feb 23, 2022) documents the 1953 founding, the founders, the South Side location, and the pre-Motown distinction.
claims.source: The Black Record Label That Introduced the Beatles to America Bryan Greene Smithsonian Magazine

claims.claim: Vee-Jay recorded Detroit-based bluesman John Lee Hooker (including the October 26, 1961 Chicago session for Burnin') and the Chicago-based Staple Singers' early gospel sides including 'Uncloudy Day.'
claims.evidence: Discographic sources document the Hooker sessions; Rob Bowman's Staple Singers biography documents the Vee-Jay gospel recordings.
claims.source: John Lee Hooker sessionography; Staple Singers biography Various; Rob Bowman discographical sources; Believers Portal
claims.uncertainty: Label-level facts are verified; specific session dates rest on discographic compilations.

entities.name: Universal Negro Improvement Association (Chicago)
entities.description: Harlem-headquartered Pan-African movement that built one of its largest divisions in Chicago's Black Belt in the early 1920s.

claims.claim: After Marcus Garvey's September 1919 Chicago visit, thousands of Black Chicagoans joined the UNIA; the Chicago division was highly regarded in the transnational movement, with Black women playing a critical organizing role.
claims.evidence: UIUC professor Erik McDuffie's study documents the mass Chicago membership and women's organizing role.
claims.source: Chicago, Garveyism, and the history of the diasporic Midwest Erik S. McDuffie UIUC African American Studies/History

claims.claim: The Chicago UNIA spawned Black nationalist political and religious movements in the city from the 1920s onward, forming a genealogy connecting Garveyism to later Black Power organizing.
claims.evidence: McDuffie's study traces the Chicago UNIA's afterlives in nationalist politics and religion.
claims.source: Chicago, Garveyism, and the history of the diasporic Midwest Erik S. McDuffie UIUC African American Studies/History

entities.name: Southern Christian Leadership Conference
entities.description: Atlanta-headquartered civil-rights organization that partnered with Chicago organizers in the 1965-66 Chicago Freedom Movement.

claims.claim: SCLC, headquartered in Atlanta, joined Chicago's Coordinating Council of Community Organizations in the Chicago Freedom Movement of 1965-66, bringing Southern movement leadership into a Northern urban campaign.
claims.evidence: A Chicago Housing Authority historical PDF and a Habitat for Humanity Portland summary document the SCLC-CCCO partnership.
claims.source: Chicago Freedom Movement history Chicago Housing Authority CHA historical PDF

entities.name: Bronzeville / Black Belt (Chicago South Side)
entities.description: Segregated South Side district that absorbed the Great Migration; documented block-by-block by Drake and Cayton's Black Metropolis (1945).

claims.claim: St. Clair Drake and Horace Cayton's Black Metropolis (1945), based on WPA fieldwork from 1936-41, documented the South Side 'Black Belt' community built by Great Migration migrants, with an introduction by Richard Wright.
claims.evidence: Yale's eHRAF World Cultures entry records the book's field dates (1936-41), Chicago coverage, and WPA basis; the KU journal article documents Wright's introduction and Drake's authorship.
claims.source: Black Metropolis: A Study of Negro Life in a Northern City St. Clair Drake and Horace R. Cayton Harcourt, Brace (1945); eHRAF/Yale

claims.claim: The Chicago Urban League, organized at the Wabash Avenue YMCA on December 11, 1916, served as the resettlement agency for arriving Southern migrants; by the mid-1960s it was headquartered in a Bronzeville mansion.
claims.evidence: Docomomo-US and the Chicago Community Trust document the December 11, 1916 organizing meeting and the Bronzeville headquarters.
