claims.evidence: BYG Records' own release page states the album was recorded at Studio Saravah, Paris, in August 1969 after the ensemble relocated to Paris.
claims.source: BYG Records, 'Message to Our Folks' release page (bygrecords.bandcamp.com)
claims.uncertainty: The Bandcamp page is undated; the August 1969 date and Studio Saravah location are not independently corroborated from session logs in this research.

claims.claim: A recording widely circulated as Art Ensemble's 'Live in Paris' (dated 5 October 1969, Paris) was in fact recorded at Châteauvallon on 13 August 1970.
claims.evidence: Discographic discussion cites France Musique and session documentation placing the recording at Châteauvallon, 13 August 1970, contradicting the Paris/5 October 1969 legend.
claims.source: Organissimo forum, 'Art Ensemble Live in Paris – is it actually Paris?' (organissimo.org)
claims.uncertainty: Evidence is a forum discussion rather than a published discography; the correction needs confirmation against session ledgers.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Commercial releases and databases continue to list the recording as 'Live in Paris', 5 October 1969.

entities.name: BYG-Actuel
entities.description: French independent record label (Paris) that documented the 1969–1971 Paris period of Chicago's avant-garde jazz musicians.

claims.claim: BYG-Actuel released the Art Ensemble of Chicago's Message to Our Folks, recorded in Paris in August 1969.
claims.evidence: BYG Records' own release page for the album records the Paris, August 1969 session at Studio Saravah.
claims.source: BYG Records, 'Message to Our Folks' release page (bygrecords.bandcamp.com)
claims.uncertainty: Release date of the album itself is not stated on the page; the session date is the documented fact.

claims.claim: BYG-Actuel released Sun Ra's The Solar-Myth Approach Vol. 1 & 2 in 1971, which introduced Ra's program to an international audience.
claims.evidence: Retailer copy states the two volumes were first released on the French label BYG/Actuel in 1971 and were essential in introducing Ra's music internationally.
claims.source: Soundohm, Sun Ra Arkestra artist page (soundohm.com)
claims.uncertainty: Retailer copy repeats label-supplied text; liner-note dates are described on the same page as 'dubious at best'.

entities.name: Memphis Slim
entities.description: Chicago blues pianist and singer (John Len Chatman, 1915–1988) who moved permanently to Paris in 1962.

claims.claim: Memphis Slim moved permanently to Paris in 1962, toured and recorded throughout Europe, and remained based there until his death in Paris on 24 February 1988.
claims.evidence: Album liner notes archived at the Internet Archive document the 1962 permanent move to Paris and his death there on 24 February 1988; French label BD Music corroborates the Paris base and European career.
claims.source: Liner notes, Internet Archive (archive.org); BD Music, 'Memphis Slim' (bdmusic.fr)
claims.uncertainty: Exact month of the 1962 move not stated in captured sources.

claims.claim: Memphis Slim performed at the first American Folk Blues Festival in 1962.
claims.evidence: The University of Mississippi's eGrove archival exhibit on the British blues explosion and the festival names Memphis Slim among the Chicago-linked artists brought to Europe.
claims.source: University of Mississippi eGrove, 'The British Blues Explosion and American Folk Blues Festival' exhibit (egrove.olemiss.edu)
claims.uncertainty: The exhibit draws on primary ephemera (programs, tickets); exact 1962 set details not captured.

entities.name: Big Bill Broonzy
entities.description: Chicago blues guitarist and singer (1893/1903–1958) whose 1950s European tours preceded and paved the way for the American Folk Blues Festival circuit.

claims.claim: Broonzy made his first tour of Europe in 1951 and toured Europe again in 1955 and 1957; his appearances introduced the blues to European audiences and were especially influential in London's emerging skiffle and blues scene.
claims.evidence: The Encyclopedia of Arkansas records the 1951 first tour and the 1955 and 1957 return tours, and notes their influence on the London scene; the Nottingham Music Archive documents a 1955 private-party performance in Nottingham and a recorded 1957 gig at the Dancing Slipper, Nottingham.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 'Broonzy, Big Bill' (encyclopediaofarkansas.net), updated 2026-09-25; Nottingham Music Archive (nottsmusicarchive.com)
claims.uncertainty: Setlist.fm lists additional dated gigs (e.g., Liverpool Cavern Club, March 1957; Copenhagen, May 1956) but is user-submitted and was not used as primary evidence.

claims.claim: The 1951 European tour came at the invitation of French critic Hugues Panassié, with performances at London's Kingsway Hall, Edinburgh's Usher Hall, and Hove Town Hall near Brighton.
claims.evidence: Blues Chronicles names Panassié as the inviter and lists those venues for the 1951 tour.
claims.source: Blues Chronicles, 'Big Bill Broonzy: The Fearless Life That Sparked New Blues' (blueschronicles.com)
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; venue-level detail not corroborated against contemporary press or Panassié's own writings.

claims.claim: Broonzy's autobiography, Big Bill Blues, was published in 1955 with the aid of Belgian writer Yannick Bruynoghe.
claims.evidence: The Encyclopedia of Arkansas records the 1955 publication with Bruynoghe; the bibliography cites the London edition (Cassell & Co., 1955).

claims.claim: While in the Netherlands, Broonzy formed a relationship with Dutch woman Pim van Isveldt; they had a child, Michael, who lives in Amsterdam.
claims.evidence: NTS's artist biography records the relationship and the child in Amsterdam.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; family details not corroborated.

entities.name: The Rolling Stones
entities.description: British rock band whose early career ran through Chicago: recording at Chess Studios and covering Chicago blues compositions.

claims.claim: The band recorded at Chess Studios, Chicago, on 10–11 June 1964, during their first American tour.
claims.evidence: Elsewhere's session history quotes Bill Wyman and Charlie Watts on the Chess recording dates.

claims.claim: Their cover of Willie Dixon's 'Little Red Rooster', recorded 2 September 1964, was released as a UK single on 13 November 1964 and reached No. 1 in December 1964.
claims.evidence: Facility Fun and Men's Journal (citing uDiscover Music) document the recording date, release date, and chart peak.
claims.uncertainty: Recording location disputed (see GBL-E-008); chart peak itself is consistent across sources.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Some sources claim a Chess Studios, Chicago recording; the two music histories place it at Regent Sound, London.

entities.name: Fleetwood Mac
entities.description: British blues-rock band that traveled to Chicago in January 1969 to record with Chess blues veterans — a documented European return flow to Chicago.

claims.claim: On 4 January 1969 Fleetwood Mac recorded at Chess's Ter-Mar studio in Chicago with Otis Spann, Willie Dixon, Shakey Horton, J.T. Brown, Buddy Guy, Honeyboy Edwards, and S.P. Leary.
claims.evidence: Discogs release metadata for the session documents the date, studio, and full personnel.
claims.uncertainty: Discogs is user-submitted; needs corroboration from Blue Horizon session documentation.

claims.claim: The session was released in December 1969 by the UK label Blue Horizon as Blues Jam at Chess.
claims.evidence: Same Discogs release metadata records the December 1969 Blue Horizon issue.
claims.uncertainty: Release month from a single discographic source.

entities.name: Olympic Sound Studios
entities.description: London recording studio where Howlin' Wolf recorded with British rock musicians in May 1970.

claims.claim: Howlin' Wolf recorded The London Howlin' Wolf Sessions at Olympic Sound Studios, London, in May 1970.
claims.evidence: Discogs release metadata documents the Olympic Sound Studios, London recording in May 1970.
claims.source: Discogs, 'The London Howlin' Wolf Sessions' release page (discogs.com)
claims.uncertainty: Discogs is user-submitted; session dates need corroboration from studio logs.

entities.name: American Folk Blues Festival
entities.description: Touring package of American blues musicians across Europe, founded 1962 by German promoters Horst Lippmann and Fritz Rau; the principal institutional pipeline for Chicago blues to Europe in the 1960s.

claims.claim: The festival was founded in 1962 by German promoters Horst Lippmann and Fritz Rau; the first edition played the Paris Olympia on 20 October 1962 and Manchester Free Trade Hall on 21 October 1962, the latter the only UK date.
claims.evidence: Louder's festival history names Lippmann and Rau as founders and gives the 1962 routing including the Olympia and Free Trade Hall dates; Bear Family's festival documentation corroborates the 1962 founding and annual touring format.
claims.uncertainty: Fritz Rau's co-founding role is documented in the festival literature but was captured here only via Louder/Bear Family summaries.

claims.claim: The University of Mississippi holds primary festival ephemera (programs, tickets, posters) and identifies Chicago-linked participants including Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Sonny Boy Williamson II, and Memphis Slim.
claims.evidence: The eGrove exhibit 'The British Blues Explosion and American Folk Blues Festival' and the Sonny Boy Williamson II exhibit present digitized programs, tickets, and posters from the university's collections.
claims.uncertainty: The exhibits were consulted via summaries; individual item-level verification of each artist's appearance was not completed.

claims.claim: The festival ran annually through the 1960s (1962–1970) with later revivals.
claims.evidence: Bear Family's multi-disc festival documentation covers the annual editions from 1962 onward.
claims.uncertainty: End date of the original annual run varies by source (1969/1970); later revival editions are documented but not dated here.

claims.claim: The festival is credited with influencing a generation of British rock musicians.
claims.evidence: Music-press histories (e.g., Louder) describe the festival's influence on British musicians, but captured sources do not provide named first-person testimony for each claimed influence.
claims.uncertainty: The 'influenced a generation' framing is broad; it should be replaced with named, dated testimony (e.g., which musician saw which edition) before being treated as fact. Scholarly work (e.g., Adelt on blues tourism) critiques romanticized versions of this narrative.

entities.name: Frankie Knuckles
entities.description: Chicago house DJ and producer (1955–2014), resident of Chicago's Warehouse; his European career ran through London's Ministry of Sound.

claims.claim: Knuckles played London's Ministry of Sound in 1992 (a set later circulated from a Hot 97 broadcast) and again in 2011.
claims.evidence: MixesDB catalogs the 1992 Ministry of Sound set with full tracklist; a DJ-sets retailer lists the 11 June 2011 Ministry of Sound set.
claims.uncertainty: Both are fan/retailer catalogs rather than venue archives; the 1992 date rests on a single catalog entry.

claims.claim: His 1991 single 'The Whistle Song' reached No. 17 in the UK; he was signed in the US and abroad to Virgin Records, the UK label founded by Richard Branson.
claims.evidence: The public-radio documentary 'Where Love Lives: Frankie Knuckles And The Dance Floor' reports the UK No. 17 peak and the Virgin Records signing.

claims.claim: Knuckles' final gig was at London's Ministry of Sound on the Saturday night before his death; the club had modeled its sound system on New York's Garage.
claims.evidence: His manager Judy Weinstein told the same public-radio documentary that he played Ministry of Sound the Saturday before he died and flew back to Chicago on Sunday; the documentary notes the club's Garage-modeled sound system.
claims.uncertainty: Red-team: 1992 date rests on fan catalog; needs venue listings.

entities.name: Marshall Jefferson
entities.description: Chicago house producer (b. 1959); 'Move Your Body' (1986) became a UK hit and a pan-European club anthem.

claims.claim: 'Move Your Body' was released on Chicago's Trax Records in 1986 (TX117) and reached No. 7 in the UK.
claims.evidence: The Jahsonic Trax discography lists TX117 as Marshall Jefferson 'Move Your Body/House Music Nat'l Anthem'; a house-history site reports the UK No. 7 peak, ahead of Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk's 'Love Can't Turn Around'.
claims.uncertainty: The UK No. 7 figure comes from a single enthusiast site and needs confirmation against Official Charts data.

claims.claim: 'Move Your Body' was an anthem at the Music Box and Power Plant in Chicago, the Paradise Garage in New York, Heaven in London, and the Palace in Paris.
claims.evidence: The same house-history account names all five clubs as rooms where the record became an anthem.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source; the claim is plausible but anecdotal.

claims.claim: Jefferson performed at the 'Haçienda 30' anniversary event at KOKO, London, on 15 December 2012, alongside Mike Pickering and Todd Terry.
claims.evidence: Plain and Simple's event listing for Haçienda 30 at KOKO names Marshall Jefferson on the bill.
claims.uncertainty: Event listing, not a review confirming the performance took place.

entities.name: Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk
entities.description: Chicago house DJ and producer (Farley Keith Williams, b. 1962); 'Love Can't Turn Around' (1986) was among the first Chicago house records to chart in the UK.

claims.claim: 'Love Can't Turn Around' (credited to Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk with Jesse Saunders, vocals by Darryl Pandy) reached No. 10 on the UK Singles Chart in 1986.
claims.evidence: MusicVF's chart archive records the UK No. 10 peak in 1986; a house-history video account independently describes it as one of the first house records to chart in the UK, peaking at number 10.
claims.source: MusicVF (musicvf.com); YouTube, 'The Late 80s: Chicago, New York, and UK House Music Grows Up' (youtube.com)
claims.uncertainty: MusicVF is a chart-data aggregator; needs confirmation against Official Charts.

entities.name: Steve 'Silk' Hurley
entities.description: Chicago house producer (b. 1962); 'Jack Your Body' (1986) was the first Chicago house record to reach No. 1 in the UK.

claims.claim: 'Jack Your Body' topped the UK Singles Chart for two weeks beginning 18 January 1987.
claims.evidence: True House Stories' interview/profile of Hurley states the record held UK No. 1 for two weeks from 18 January 1987.
claims.uncertainty: The claim rests on an artist interview; it needs confirmation against Official Charts data before being treated as settled.

claims.claim: 'Jack Your Body' appeared on the 1986 compilation The House Sound of Chicago.
claims.evidence: A discographic upload of the DJ International compilation lists 'Jack Your Body' as the opening track.
claims.source: YouTube, 'House Sound of Chicago DJ International 1986' (youtube.com)
claims.uncertainty: Tracklist from a fan upload of the cassette; label copy not consulted.

entities.name: Lil Louis
entities.description: Chicago house producer (Louis Burns, b. 1962); 'French Kiss' (1989) reached No. 2 in the UK.

claims.claim: 'French Kiss' reached No. 2 on the UK Singles Chart in 1989.
claims.evidence: MusicVF's chart archive records the UK No. 2 peak in 1989.
claims.uncertainty: Single chart-aggregator source; needs confirmation against Official Charts.

entities.name: Roy Davis Jr.
entities.description: Chicago house producer; 'Gabriel' (1997) was licensed from Chicago's Large Records to the UK's XL Recordings and became a UK Top 25 hit.

claims.claim: 'Gabrielle' (with vocals by Chicago singer Peven Everett) was released on Chicago's Large Records in 1996.
claims.evidence: Discogs release data for the Large Records issue documents the 1996 Chicago release and Everett's vocal credit.
claims.uncertainty: Discogs is user-submitted; label catalog confirmation needed.

claims.claim: The UK's XL Recordings licensed the track and released it as 'Gabriel' in October 1997; it reached No. 22 on the UK Singles Chart in November 1997 and was named NME Single of the Week.
claims.evidence: Discogs documents the XL Recordings release; chart and NME details were captured from discographic and press summaries in session research.
claims.uncertainty: Chart position and NME citation rest on a single discographic source; needs Official Charts and NME archive confirmation.

entities.name: DJ Rush
entities.description: Chicago-born techno DJ and producer (Isaiah Major) who relocated to Berlin, where his European career took off.

claims.claim: DJ Rush is from Chicago, made his way to Berlin, Germany, where his career 'kicked off into high gear', and lived in Berlin ('when I used to live there').
claims.evidence: In a Tanzgemeinschaft interview, Rush describes himself as an American DJ from Chicago, states he found his way to Berlin and his career took off there, and refers to living in Berlin around the Love Parade era.
claims.source: Tanzgemeinschaft, 'DJ Rush Shares His Thoughts On His Love for Techno' (tanzgemeinschaft.com) — artist interview
claims.uncertainty: The interview does not date the move; the 1996 date below comes from a separate source.

claims.claim: Rush moved to Berlin in 1996, established the Kne'Deep label/agency there, had a Europe-wide breakthrough in 1998, and was Groove Magazine's reader's choice in 2001.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia's DJ Rush article records the 1996 Berlin move, the Kne'Deep imprint, the 1998 breakthrough, and the 2001 Groove poll.
claims.uncertainty: Wikipedia is the sole source for the dates and label details; treat as provisional pending interview or press corroboration.

claims.claim: Rush hosted his own tents/stages at Tomorrowland (Belgium), Dance Valley (Netherlands), and Summer Spirit (Germany).
claims.evidence: The Tanzgemeinschaft interview states he hosted his own tents at all three European festivals.
claims.uncertainty: Artist's own account; years not specified.

entities.name: Honey Dijon
entities.description: Chicago-born DJ, producer, and fashion-world figure based between New York and Berlin; a continuing Chicago-to-Europe house lineage.

claims.claim: Dijon splits her time between New York and Berlin and has played Berghain and Panorama Bar in Berlin.

claims.uncertainty: Residency details are as reported in interviews; no fixed Berlin move date captured.

entities.name: DJ Rashad
entities.description: Chicago footwork producer (Rashad Harden, 1979–2014) whose music reached European audiences through the UK label Planet Mu.

claims.claim: DJ Rashad was a featured artist on Planet Mu's Bangs & Works Vol. 1 (A Chicago Footwork Compilation), released 6 December 2010.

entities.name: Planet Mu
entities.description: UK independent electronic-music label that released the Chicago footwork compilations Bangs & Works and brought footwork artists to European audiences.

entities.name: XL Recordings
entities.description: UK record label that licensed Roy Davis Jr.'s Chicago house record 'Gabriel' for the British market in 1997.

claims.evidence: Discogs release data documents the XL Recordings UK release; chart and date details captured from discographic summaries in session research.
claims.uncertainty: Licensing terms not documented; chart position needs Official Charts confirmation.

entities.name: The Haçienda
entities.description: Manchester nightclub (Factory Records, 1982–1997) that became one of the first British clubs to play Chicago house music in 1986.

claims.claim: In 1986 the Haçienda became one of the first British clubs to play house music, with DJs Hewan Clarke, Greg Wilson, and later Mike Pickering and Little Martin hosting the Friday 'Nude' night built around imported Chicago (and New York) house records.
claims.evidence: The club's history records the 1986 shift and the Nude night's resident DJs; Decoded Magazine, reviewing Mike Pickering's memoir (Manchester University Press, April 2026), describes Nude as 'among the first club nights in the UK to commit seriously to imported Chicago and New York house records'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The Haçienda' (en.wikipedia.org); Decoded Magazine, 'Book of the Month: Manchester must dance' (decodedmagazine.com), 2026
claims.uncertainty: Wikipedia is one of two sources here and is not the sole source; the memoir review provides the stronger corroboration.

entities.name: Ministry of Sound
entities.description: London nightclub that hosted Chicago house pioneer Frankie Knuckles repeatedly, including his final performance.

claims.claim: Frankie Knuckles played Ministry of Sound, London, in 1992 (a set later circulated via a Hot 97 broadcast) and his final gig there on the Saturday night before his death in 2014.
claims.evidence: MixesDB catalogs the 1992 set; the public-radio documentary 'Where Love Lives' reports, via his manager Judy Weinstein, that he played Ministry of Sound the Saturday before he died and flew back to Chicago on Sunday.
claims.source: MixesDB (mixesdb.com); KTTZ / public radio, 'Where Love Lives' (radio.kttz.org), 2014-04-02
claims.uncertainty: The 1992 set date rests on a fan catalog; the final-gig account is via the manager's testimony.

entities.name: Archibald Motley
entities.description: Chicago painter (1891–1981) of the Black Chicago Renaissance; painted his noted work Blues while on fellowship in Paris.

claims.claim: Motley received a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1929, spent 1929 to early 1930 in Paris, and painted Blues there.
claims.evidence: The Nasher Museum (Duke University) exhibition on Motley and a Whitney Museum publication both document the 1929 Guggenheim Fellowship, the Paris stay, and the painting of Blues in Paris.
claims.source: Nasher Museum of Art, 'Archibald Motley: Jazz Age Modernist' (nasher.duke.edu); Whitney Museum publication (whitney.org)

entities.name: Lorraine Hansberry
entities.description: Chicago-born playwright (1930–1965); her Chicago-set A Raisin in the Sun had its European premiere in England in 1959.

claims.claim: Hansberry was born in Chicago on 19 May 1930 and set A Raisin in the Sun in Chicago.

claims.source: Humanists UK, 'A Raisin in the Sun' (heritage.humanists.uk)
claims.uncertainty: Single UK heritage source; theatre-archive corroboration would strengthen it.

entities.name: Theaster Gates
entities.description: Chicago artist and urban planner (b. 1973); represented Chicago's South Side at dOCUMENTA 13 in Kassel, Germany, in 2012.

claims.claim: At dOCUMENTA 13 (Kassel, Germany, 2012), Gates presented 12 Ballads for Huguenot House, for which materials from 6901 South Dorchester Avenue in Chicago were transported to Kassel and rebuilt as the 'Huguenot House'.
claims.evidence: Nonsite's essay on Gates documents the dOCUMENTA 13 project and the use of materials from 6901 South Dorchester; Gates's own Wallpaper interview corroborates the Kassel project.
claims.source: Nonsite, 'Theaster Gates: Social Formations' (nonsite.org); Wallpaper, 'At Home with Theaster Gates' interview (wallpaper.com)

claims.claim: The Huguenot House hosted performances by Gates's ensemble the Black Monks of Mississippi during dOCUMENTA 13.
claims.evidence: Nonsite documents the Black Monks performances at the Kassel site.
claims.uncertainty: Single secondary source for the performance detail.

entities.name: Loleatta Holloway
entities.description: Chicago-born singer (1946–2011) whose recording was sampled without clearance by the Italian group Black Box — a documented Europe-to-Chicago rights dispute.

claims.claim: The Italian group Black Box sampled Holloway's 'Love Sensation' without clearance for their 1989 hit 'Ride on Time'; Holloway sued.
claims.evidence: NME's 30-year retrospective on 'Ride on Time' reports the unlicensed sampling of 'Love Sensation' and Holloway's lawsuit.
claims.source: NME, '30 Years: Full Story of Ride on Time' (nme.com), 2019
claims.uncertainty: Settlement terms not captured; the lawsuit outcome is not documented here.

claims.claim: This is a documented Europe–Chicago rights flow (Italian producers sampling a Chicago-born singer), but Holloway should not be framed as a Chicago house producer; she was a disco/soul vocalist.
claims.evidence: NME and biographical sources describe Holloway as a disco/soul singer; the sampling case is the documented link.

entities.name: The House Sound of Chicago
entities.description: 1986 compilation of Chicago house records that circulated in the UK through London Records.

claims.claim: The House Sound of Chicago was released in 1986 on Chicago's DJ International label and was available in the UK through London Records; its tracklist included Steve 'Silk' Hurley's 'Jack Your Body', Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk's 'Love Can't Turn Around', and Marshall Jefferson's 'Move Your Body'.

claims.claim: Pete Tong's biography credits him and London Records with organizing the 1986 compilation, described as the first British compilation focused on Chicago house.

claims.uncertainty: Commercial biography copy; 'first British compilation' is a promotional framing that conflicts with the DJ International origin evidence.

claims.claim: Under John H. Sengstacke, the Defender network acquired the Michigan Chronicle (Detroit), the Pittsburgh Courier (Pittsburgh), and the Tri-State Defender (Memphis, Tennessee).

claims.claim: Bishop William Paul Quinn organized AME churches across Indiana, Illinois, and Missouri; Quinn Chapel's congregation joined the AME in 1847.
claims.evidence: Chicago Public Library's Quinn Chapel archive finding aid.
claims.uncertainty: Low for Quinn's regional church organizing; direct interaction among those specific churches is not documented.

claims.claim: Members of Quinn Chapel were instrumental in founding Provident Hospital, the Elam House, and the Wabash Avenue YMCA.
claims.evidence: HABS significance statement (via Library of Congress) credits Quinn congregation members with these foundings; no independent corroboration found in this round.
claims.uncertainty: High: single-source attribution.

claims.claim: In 1992 Quinn Chapel joined three other nearby churches to found the Renaissance Collaborative to save the historic Wabash YMCA.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia summaries of Quinn Chapel's history.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: encyclopedia-only in this round.

claims.claim: The NACW held its second national convention at Quinn Chapel AME Church, Chicago, August 14–16, 1899.
claims.evidence: Digitized primary minutes of the 1899 convention (Colored Conventions Project, Omeka item 558).
claims.uncertainty: Low: primary source.

claims.claim: Olivet Baptist Church was a venue for the National Baptist Convention's 1943 annual session in Chicago.
claims.evidence: Contemporaneous Smithsonian primary artifact: a form letter naming the U.S. Armory, Olivet Baptist, Pilgrim Baptist, and Monumental Baptist as venues for the September 7–12, 1943 convention.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Olivet pastors Lacey Kirk Williams and Joseph H. Jackson each became president of the National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc., making Olivet a platform for national denominational leadership.
claims.evidence: Preservation Chicago documents Williams's 1916 arrival from Texas and NBC presidency and Jackson's 1941 pastorate and NBC presidency; start years for the presidencies conflict across sources (Williams 1922 vs. 1924; Jackson 1953 vs. 1954).
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: presidency start years conflict; the leadership link itself is consistent across sources.

claims.claim: Williams came from Texas to pastor Olivet Baptist Church in Chicago in 1916 and served as president of the National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc. (sources give 1922 or 1924 through 1940).
claims.evidence: Preservation Chicago; NBC chronology mirrors.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: presidency start year conflicts (1922 vs. 1924).
claims.contradictory_evidence: Some sources give 1922, others 1924 as the start of his NBC presidency.

claims.claim: Jackson became pastor of Olivet Baptist Church in 1941 and served as president of the National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc. (sources give 1953 or 1954 through 1982).
claims.evidence: Preservation Chicago; NBC chronology mirrors.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: presidency start year conflicts (1953 vs. 1954).
claims.contradictory_evidence: Some sources give 1953, others 1954 as the start of his NBC presidency.

claims.claim: At the 1915 NBC annual meeting in Chicago, confrontations over the National Baptist Publishing Board led R. H. Boyd and his supporters to form the National Baptist Convention of America; the remaining convention incorporated in 1916 as the National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc.
claims.evidence: R. H. Boyd encyclopedia article and the NBC USA chronology both place the 1915 confrontation and split at the Chicago annual meeting.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: Wikipedia is the lead source but is corroborated by the NBC USA chronology text.

claims.claim: The NBC held its annual session in Chicago, September 7–12, 1943, using the U.S. Armory, Olivet Baptist, Pilgrim Baptist, and Monumental Baptist as venues.
claims.evidence: Contemporaneous Smithsonian primary artifact (form letter, NMAAHC 2017.14.9).
claims.uncertainty: Low; attendance totals were not found and are not claimed.

claims.claim: The NBCA was formed in Chicago in 1915 by R. H. Boyd and his supporters after the split with the National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc.
claims.evidence: R. H. Boyd encyclopedia article; NBC USA chronology mirror.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate.

claims.claim: The PNBC held its 64th Annual Session in Chicago, July 20–23, 2025, at McCormick Place, drawing about 2,000 delegates.
claims.evidence: PNBC's official program update ('All roads lead to Chicago, IL July 20-23, 2025, for the 64th PNBC Annual Session at the McCormick Place Convention Center') and Religion News Service coverage of the session.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Thomas A. Dorsey served as music director at Pilgrim Baptist Church; the Smithsonian identifies Pilgrim as the birthplace of gospel music.
claims.evidence: NMAAHC object record: Dorsey as Pilgrim's music director and Pilgrim as birthplace of gospel music, with artists including Mahalia Jackson, Sallie Martin, Aretha Franklin, James Cleveland, the Staple Singers, and the Edwin Hawkins Singers.
claims.uncertainty: Low.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Competing historiography: Charles Albert Tindley is widely credited as "father of American gospel music," predating Dorsey's 1930s Chicago work; "birthplace"/"father of" titles are contested honorifics.

claims.claim: Pilgrim was a venue for the National Baptist Convention's 1943 annual session in Chicago.
claims.evidence: Contemporaneous Smithsonian primary artifact (form letter, NMAAHC 2017.14.9).
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Pastor Junius C. Austin established missions in Africa under Pilgrim's ministry.
claims.evidence: A Congressional Record tribute states Austin established missions in Africa; no independent corroboration found in this research round.
claims.uncertainty: High: single-source tribute claim; institutional boosterism risk.

entities.name: National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses (NCGCC)

claims.claim: The NCGCC organized its first session at Pilgrim Baptist Church, Chicago, on August 30, 1933, following the formation of a Chicago choral union in 1932.
claims.evidence: Secondary promotional coverage of NCGCC history.
claims.uncertainty: High: promotional sources only; founding minutes not located in this round. Institutional boosterism risk.

claims.claim: The NCGCC continues to rotate its annual sessions across cities (e.g., the 84th annual session in Baltimore).
claims.evidence: Coverage of the 84th annual session in Baltimore.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate.

entities.name: Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ

claims.claim: Roberts Temple was COGIC's Northern Illinois 'Mother Church'; Emmett Till's body was returned from Mississippi to Chicago and his funeral was held at Roberts Temple on September 3, 1955.
claims.evidence: Federal Register (2023): Till's body returned from Mississippi to Chicago; funeral at Roberts Temple on September 3, 1955; Roberts Temple described as COGIC's Northern Illinois 'Mother Church.'
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Ford pastored Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ in Chicago and delivered the eulogy at Emmett Till's 1955 funeral, attended by 2,000 mourners inside and thousands outside.
claims.evidence: Senate source: Isaiah Roberts presided, Ford delivered the eulogy, 2,000 mourners inside and thousands outside.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Ford later became Presiding Bishop of the Church of God in Christ (Tennessee Encyclopedia gives 1989; a secondary source gives 1990–1995), before Chandler Owens (1995).
claims.evidence: Tennessee Encyclopedia: 'Louis H. Ford and Chandler Owens occupied the Presiding Bishopric in 1989 and 1995, respectively.'
claims.uncertainty: Low for Ford's tenure; exact start year varies (1989 vs. 1990).
claims.contradictory_evidence: Secondary sources give 1990 or 1995 as start; Tennessee Encyclopedia gives 1989.

claims.claim: COGIC was founded in 1907; its world headquarters are in Memphis, Tennessee, and Roberts Temple is its Northern Illinois 'Mother Church.'
claims.evidence: Federal Register (2023) and Tennessee Encyclopedia.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Noble Drew Ali established a Canaanite Temple in Newark, New Jersey in 1913 and moved the movement's headquarters to Chicago in 1925, incorporating in Illinois in 1926/1928.
claims.evidence: EBSCO Research Starter on Noble Drew Ali; CSU master's thesis.
claims.uncertainty: Low for the Newark-to-Chicago headquarters transfer; incorporation year given as 1926 or 1928 across sources.

claims.claim: The MSTA held its Moorish National Conclave in Chicago in October 1928 and published the Moorish Guide, reported to reach at least twelve states.
claims.evidence: CSU master's thesis and secondary summaries.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: single thesis source for the conclave; state-reach figure is reported, not independently confirmed.

claims.claim: Drew Ali founded the Moorish Science Temple movement in Newark in 1913 and moved its headquarters to Chicago in 1925.
claims.evidence: EBSCO Research Starter; CSU master's thesis.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: North Star Lodge No. 12/No. 1 of Chicago was organized by the Ohio Jurisdiction in 1852; the Illinois Grand Lodge was organized in 1867.
claims.evidence: Illinois Prince Hall Masonic journal (primary institutional publication).
claims.uncertainty: Low for the organizational history; modern international-interaction claims in the same journal are caption-based and treated cautiously.

claims.claim: UNIA Division 23 was founded in Chicago in 1920, established its Liberty Hall at 4859 South State Street, and claimed more than 20,000 members, making it the second-largest UNIA division in the world after Harlem.
claims.evidence: Peer-reviewed-adjacent working paper on Garveyism in the Midwest, citing Robert A. Hill's Marcus Garvey and UNIA Papers.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: membership counts are the division's own claims.

claims.claim: By 1930 the UNIA had established nine divisions in the Chicago area, including three in the city itself.
claims.evidence: Same Midwest Garveyism working paper.
claims.uncertainty: Moderate.

claims.claim: The Wabash Avenue YMCA (founded 1915) was the first YMCA in the Midwest to serve people of color and a hub of Great Migration services.
claims.evidence: Bronzeville Black Metropolis National Heritage Area press release; PFA Foundation history.
claims.uncertainty: Low for the founding and first-in-Midwest claim.

claims.claim: Carter G. Woodson founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History at the Wabash YMCA on September 9, 1915.
claims.evidence: ASALH's own timeline and the PFA Foundation.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Association for the Study of Negro Life and History (ASNLH/ASALH)

claims.claim: Carter G. Woodson, George Cleveland Hall, W. B. Hartgrove, Alexander L. Jackson, and James E. Stamps founded the ASNLH in Chicago on September 9, 1915, after a meeting at the Wabash YMCA.
claims.evidence: ASALH's official Carter G. Woodson timeline.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: The ASNLH was incorporated in Washington, D.C. on October 2, 1915, within a month of its Chicago founding.
claims.evidence: ASALH's official timeline.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Wells founded the Alpha Suffrage Club in Chicago in 1913; it orchestrated the election of Chicago's first Black alderman, Oscar DePriest, in 1914.
claims.evidence: University of Arkansas profile of Wells.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP)

claims.claim: In 1912 the NAACP added its first two branches in Boston and Chicago.
claims.evidence: NAACP organizational history: 'In 1912, the organization added its first branches in Boston and Chicago.'
claims.uncertainty: Moderate: encyclopedia-only in this round; the claim is specific and widely repeated but lacks a primary citation here.

claims.claim: Wells was a founder of the NAACP in 1909 but never took an active role in it.
claims.evidence: Tennessee State Museum and USC biographies.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.location: New York, New York (headquarters); Chicago branch

claims.claim: Provident Hospital was founded in Chicago in 1891 by Dr. Daniel Hale Williams as the first Black-owned and operated hospital in the United States, with a Training School for Nurses.
claims.evidence: Chicago History Museum: founded 1891 by Dr. Daniel Hale Williams; first Black-owned/operated hospital; first nursing class included Emma Reynolds.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Dr. Austin Curtis trained at Provident from 1891 to 1893 and became the first Black surgeon-in-chief at Freedmen's Hospital in Washington, D.C., carrying Provident's training model to the national capital.
claims.evidence: Northwestern University Galter Health Sciences Library biography of Austin Curtis.
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Payne worked for the Chicago Defender from 1951, took its Washington bureau (1953 or 1954), attended the April 1955 Bandung Conference with Richard Wright, and accompanied Nixon to Ghanaian independence, later reporting from Vietnam.
claims.evidence: National Press Club; James McGrath Morris biography synopsis; postal-history PDF with Ghana detail.
claims.uncertainty: Low for Bandung and Ghana; the Washington bureau start year conflicts (1953 vs. 1954).
claims.contradictory_evidence: Sources conflict on whether she took the bureau in 1953 or 1954.
